phy_edx.5.4.summary: Unstable nuclei emit three main kinds of nuclear radiation: an **alpha particle** (equivalent to a **helium nucleus**, 2 protons and 2 neutrons), a **beta particle** (an **electron emitted from the nucleus**; the beta-plus version is a positron) and a **gamma ray** (**electromagnetic radiation**). They differ in charge and mass, which explains how strongly they **ionise** and how far they **penetrate**. Alpha is the most ionising but least penetrating (stopped by paper), beta is in between (stopped by a few mm of aluminium) and gamma is the least ionising but most penetrating (only reduced by several cm of lead).

core.h: Three kinds of radiation from the nucleus
core.p: All three types are given out by **unstable nuclei** as they decay. They are all **ionising radiations**, but they are very different things: two are particles with mass and charge, one is a wave.
bullets: **Alpha (α)**: a particle equivalent to a **helium nucleus**
**Beta (β- )**: a fast **electron emitted from the nucleus**
**Positron (β+)**: the positive version of beta, a positron emitted from the nucleus
**Gamma (γ)**: a high-frequency **electromagnetic wave**
Their **charge**, **mass** and **energy** decide how they behave in matter

callouts.p: An alpha particle is equivalent to a helium nucleus; a beta particle is an electron emitted from the nucleus; a gamma ray is electromagnetic radiation.

core.p: An alpha particle is made of **2 protons and 2 neutrons** bound together, exactly the same as the nucleus of a helium atom. It has no electrons, so it carries a **charge of +2**.
bullets: Relative mass **4**, relative charge **+2**
Symbol: 4 over 2 He (or 4 over 2 α)
The **heaviest** and **most highly charged** radiation
Moves relatively slowly compared with beta and gamma
**Strongly ionising**; **weakly penetrating**
Range of only a **few cm in air**; stopped by a **sheet of paper** or the outer layer of dead skin

callouts.p: Do not write 'a helium atom'. It is a helium nucleus: it has no electrons.

core.p: A beta-minus particle is a **high-speed electron that comes from the nucleus**, not from the electron shells. It is created when a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton. A beta-plus particle is a **positron**: the same mass as an electron but a positive charge.
bullets: Beta-minus: relative charge **-1**, relative mass about **1/1840** (almost zero)
Positron (beta-plus): relative charge **+1**, same tiny mass
Symbol for beta-minus: 0 over -1 e; for a positron: 0 over +1 e
**Moderately ionising** and **moderately penetrating**
Range up to about **a metre in air**; passes through paper; stopped by **a few mm of aluminium**

callouts.p: The beta electron is made in and emitted from the nucleus. The atom's orbiting electrons are not involved.

core.p: Gamma rays are **electromagnetic radiation** of very high frequency and very short wavelength, at the top end of the electromagnetic spectrum. They are emitted when a nucleus gets rid of extra energy, often just after an alpha or beta decay.
bullets: **No mass** and **no charge**
Travel at the **speed of light** (3 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum)
Emitting gamma does **not change** the mass number or atomic number
**Weakly ionising**; **highly penetrating**
Passes through paper and aluminium; intensity only **reduced** by **several cm of lead** or **thick concrete**
Travels a very long way in air

core.p: This is the table to learn by heart. Exam questions often give part of it with gaps.
bullets: Pattern: as you go alpha to beta to gamma, **ionising power falls** and **penetrating power rises**

core.p: Radiation **ionises** an atom when it knocks one or more **electrons** out of it, leaving a **positive ion**. Every ionisation uses up some of the radiation's energy. So ionising and penetrating are connected: the more ionisations per centimetre, the faster the energy is used up and the shorter the distance travelled.
bullets: Ionisation = removing electrons from atoms to form ions
Each collision transfers energy from the radiation to the material
When all its energy is used, the radiation is **absorbed** (stopped)
Ionisation in living cells can damage DNA, which is why radiation is dangerous

callouts.p: How readily the radiation knocks electrons out of atoms it passes, forming ions.
How far the radiation can travel through a material before it is absorbed.

core.h: Why alpha is so strongly ionising
core.p: Alpha particles are **large**, **slow** and carry a **+2 charge**. The strong charge pulls hard on electrons in nearby atoms, and because the particle moves slowly it spends longer near each atom. It therefore produces a huge number of ions in a short distance.
bullets: Large charge (+2): strong electrostatic pull on electrons
Large mass and relatively slow: more time near each atom
Many ionisations per mm, so it **loses its energy very quickly**
Result: **short range** - stopped by paper or a few cm of air

callouts.p: Say: 'alpha is the most ionising, so it transfers its energy quickly and is stopped in a short distance - that is why it is the least penetrating'.

core.p: Gamma rays have **no charge** and **no mass**, so they rarely interact with the atoms they pass. They produce very few ions per cm, lose energy slowly and can travel through a lot of material.
bullets: No charge: no electrostatic pull on electrons
Few interactions, so **weakly ionising**
Energy lost slowly, so **highly penetrating**
Lead is a good absorber because it is very **dense** with lots of electrons to interact with
Gamma is never completely 'stopped' - the intensity is reduced

core.p: Beta particles have a **smaller charge (-1)** than alpha and a **tiny mass**, and they travel very fast. They ionise less often than alpha, so they travel further, but they are charged so they still ionise more than gamma.
bullets: Charge -1, so weaker interaction than alpha
Very fast and very light: less time near each atom
Moderately ionising, so moderately penetrating
Stopped by a few mm of aluminium

callouts.p: The more strongly a radiation ionises, the less penetrating it is.

core.p: You can work out which radiation a source emits by placing different absorbers between the source and a **GM tube** and seeing what makes the count rate fall.
bullets: Measure the **background count rate** first and subtract it from every reading
Keep the **distance** between source and detector fixed (alpha only travels a few cm, so keep it close)
Record the count rate with **no absorber**, then **paper**, **aluminium (few mm)**, **lead (few cm)**
Big drop with paper: **alpha** present
Further drop with aluminium: **beta** present
Count that remains through aluminium and is reduced by lead: **gamma** present
Use tongs, keep the source away from the body, return it to its lead box quickly

head: Count rate falls when you add...
Radiation present
rows: Still a count after aluminium, reduced by lead

callouts.p: If the count rate after lead equals the background, there is no gamma - not 'lead stopped everything'.

core.h: Charge shown by deflection in fields
core.p: Because alpha and beta are charged, they are **deflected** by electric and magnetic fields; gamma is not. This is evidence for their charges.
bullets: Alpha (+) bends **towards the negative plate**
Beta-minus (-) bends **towards the positive plate**, in the opposite direction to alpha
Beta is deflected **much more** than alpha because its mass is so much smaller
Gamma is **not deflected** because it has no charge

core.h: Using the properties to explain hazards and uses
core.p: Many exam questions ask you to apply ionising and penetrating power to a situation.
bullets: **Outside the body**: alpha is stopped by skin, so least harmful; beta and gamma can reach organs
**Inside the body** (swallowed or breathed in): alpha is most harmful because it is the most ionising and all its energy is deposited in a small region of cells
Smoke detectors use alpha because it ionises air strongly but cannot escape the casing
Paper thickness gauges use beta because it partly passes through paper
Medical tracers and sterilising use gamma because it can pass out of the body or through packaging

callouts.p: Pick the radiation whose penetration matches the job, then justify with ionising/penetrating power.

analogy.t: Bowling ball, tennis ball and ghost
analogy.p: Imagine running through a crowded room. Alpha is a huge, slow bowling ball with a strong pull: it crashes into everyone near it (lots of ionising) but stops after a few steps (low penetration). Beta is a fast tennis ball: it hits fewer people and gets further. Gamma is almost a ghost: it rarely touches anyone, so it gets right across the room. The analogy breaks down because gamma is a wave, not a ball, and radiation does not bounce off people - it removes electrons from atoms and transfers energy each time.

terms.d: Two protons and two neutrons; equivalent to a helium nucleus; charge +2, mass 4.
A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus; charge -1, very small mass.
A particle with the mass of an electron and charge +1, emitted from the nucleus.
High-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted from a nucleus; no mass, no charge.
A nucleus that may decay by emitting radiation to become more stable.
Removing electrons from atoms (or molecules) so that they become ions.
An atom that has lost or gained electrons, so it is charged.
How strongly radiation ionises atoms it passes; alpha strongest, gamma weakest.
How far radiation travels through a material before being absorbed; gamma most, alpha least.
Material placed in the path of radiation to absorb it, e.g. paper, aluminium, lead.
The distance radiation travels in a material before being absorbed.
Transverse waves of electric and magnetic fields travelling at the speed of light.
Charge compared with a proton: alpha +2, beta -1, positron +1, gamma 0.
Number of counts per second or per minute recorded by a detector.

mistakes.w: An alpha particle is a helium atom.
mistakes.r: It is a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons, no electrons).

mistakes.w: A beta particle is an electron from the outer shell of the atom.
mistakes.r: A beta particle is an electron emitted from the nucleus.

mistakes.w: Gamma is a particle with no mass.
mistakes.r: Gamma is electromagnetic radiation (a wave).

mistakes.w: Gamma is the most ionising because it is the most dangerous.
mistakes.r: Gamma is the least ionising; alpha is the most ionising.

mistakes.w: Lead stops gamma completely.
mistakes.r: Several cm of lead greatly reduces (absorbs most of) gamma.

mistakes.w: Beta is stopped by paper.
mistakes.r: Beta passes through paper; it is stopped by a few mm of aluminium.

mistakes.w: Alpha is the most penetrating because it is the biggest.
mistakes.r: Alpha is the least penetrating because it ionises strongly and loses its energy quickly.

mistakes.w: Alpha is harmless.
mistakes.r: Alpha is harmless only outside the body; inside the body it is the most dangerous.

mistakes.w: Forgetting background in absorber experiments.
mistakes.r: Subtract the background count rate from each reading.

exam.q: State what an alpha particle is.
model: A helium nucleus / 2 protons and 2 neutrons
exam.tip: 'Helium atom' gets zero.

exam.q: State what a beta-minus particle is.
model: An electron emitted from the nucleus (fast-moving)
exam.tip: Include 'from the nucleus'.

exam.q: Which type of radiation is part of the electromagnetic spectrum?
model: Gamma
exam.tip: Alpha and beta are particles.

exam.q: Which radiation is the most ionising? Give a reason.
model: Alpha
It has the largest charge (+2) / largest mass so interacts strongly with atoms
exam.tip: Reason must refer to charge or mass.

exam.q: State what is needed to absorb (a) alpha (b) beta (c) gamma radiation.
model: (a) paper / a few cm of air / skin
(b) a few mm of aluminium
(c) several cm of lead / thick concrete (reduces it)
exam.tip: Give a material and a thickness.

exam.q: Explain why alpha radiation has a much shorter range in air than gamma radiation.
model: Alpha is strongly ionising (gamma weakly ionising)
Each ionisation transfers energy, so alpha loses its energy quickly
So alpha is stopped after a short distance; gamma loses energy slowly and travels much further
exam.tip: The chain: ionise, lose energy, stop.

exam.q: A source is placed 3 cm from a GM tube. Corrected count rates: no absorber 400 counts/s, paper 400 counts/s, 3 mm aluminium 120 counts/s, 2 cm lead 30 counts/s. Which radiations does the source emit? Explain.
model: No alpha: paper causes no drop
Beta present: aluminium reduces count rate a lot
Gamma present: count rate still present after aluminium
Lead reduces the gamma (but does not stop it)
exam.tip: Work through each absorber in turn.

exam.q: Compare the ionising and penetrating abilities of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
model: Alpha most ionising, gamma least ionising, beta in between
Alpha least penetrating (stopped by paper)
Beta moderately penetrating (stopped by a few mm aluminium)
Gamma most penetrating (reduced by thick lead); the more ionising the less penetrating
exam.tip: 'Compare' needs comparative words for both properties.

exam.q: Explain why a beam of radiation from a source splits into three when it passes between charged plates.
model: Alpha is positive so is deflected towards the negative plate
Beta is negative so is deflected towards the positive plate, more than alpha (smaller mass)
Gamma has no charge so is not deflected
exam.tip: Link each deflection to charge.

exam.q: Explain why alpha sources are dangerous inside the body but much less dangerous outside it.
model: Outside, alpha is absorbed by the dead outer layer of skin/clothes so cannot reach living cells
Inside, alpha is highly ionising so it damages the nearby cells strongly
exam.tip: Use ionising and penetrating in the same answer.

exam.q: Describe how you would use a GM tube and absorbers to find out which type(s) of radiation a sealed source emits. Include how you would make the results valid and how you would work safely. (6 marks)
model: Measure background count rate with source absent
Place source a short fixed distance (a few cm) from GM tube; measure count rate with no absorber
Repeat with paper, then a few mm of aluminium, then several cm of lead
Subtract background from each reading; repeat and average (decay is random)
Drop with paper means alpha; drop with aluminium means beta; count remaining through aluminium, reduced by lead, means gamma
Safety: handle with tongs, keep at arm's length, minimise exposure time, store in lead box
exam.tip: Cover method, analysis and safety for full marks.

worked.q: A source gives these readings (counts per minute): background 20; no absorber 520; paper 515; 5 mm aluminium 22; 5 cm lead 21. Identify the radiation.
steps: Correct each reading: no absorber 500, paper 495, aluminium 2, lead 1
Paper hardly changes the count (495 vs 500, within random variation): no alpha
Aluminium reduces the count almost to zero: beta present
After aluminium the corrected count is about zero: no gamma
worked.ans: The source emits beta radiation only.

worked.q: Explain, using ionising and penetrating power, why gamma is used to sterilise sealed packs of surgical instruments rather than alpha.
steps: The radiation must pass through the packaging to reach microorganisms on the instruments
Alpha is weakly penetrating and would be absorbed by the packaging
Gamma is highly penetrating so it passes through the packaging and kills the microorganisms
worked.ans: Gamma, because only it penetrates the sealed packaging; the pack can stay sealed so the instruments stay sterile.

worked.q: Compare the relative charge and mass of an alpha and a beta-minus particle, and use this to explain which is deflected more in an electric field.
steps: Alpha: charge +2, mass 4; beta: charge -1, mass about 1/1840
Alpha has twice the charge but about 7000 times the mass
Force depends on charge; a large mass makes a particle much harder to deflect
worked.ans: Beta is deflected much more (in the opposite direction to alpha) because its mass is so small.

phy_edx.5.5.summary: The model of the atom has changed as **new experimental evidence** appeared. Dalton's solid sphere was replaced by Thomson's **plum pudding model** (a ball of positive charge with electrons embedded in it) after the electron was discovered. Rutherford's **alpha particle scattering experiment** showed that most of the atom is empty space with a tiny, dense, positive **nucleus**, giving the nuclear model, and **Bohr** then improved it by placing electrons in **fixed orbits (energy levels)** at set distances from the nucleus.

core.p: A scientific model is a simplified picture used to explain observations and make predictions. When an experiment produces results that a model **cannot explain**, scientists change or replace the model. The atom is the classic example: each new model was accepted because it explained more of the evidence.
bullets: A model must explain **all** the available evidence
New technology allows new experiments, giving **new evidence**
If results do not match a model's **predictions**, the model is changed
New ideas are checked by other scientists (**peer review**) and by repeating experiments
Old models are not 'wrong and useless' - they were the best explanation for the evidence at the time

callouts.p: Describe how and why the atomic model has changed, including the plum pudding model and Rutherford alpha particle scattering leading to the Bohr model.

core.p: In the early 1800s John Dalton described atoms as **tiny solid spheres** that could not be divided, with each element having its own kind of atom.
bullets: Atoms were thought to be **indivisible** (could not be split)
Different elements had different atoms
No idea of any particles inside the atom

core.h: Discovery of the electron and the plum pudding model
core.p: In 1897 **J.J. Thomson** discovered the **electron**, a tiny negatively charged particle that came from inside atoms. So atoms could not be indivisible. Since atoms are neutral overall, there had to be **positive charge** too. Thomson proposed the **plum pudding model**.
bullets: Atom = a **ball of positive charge**
**Negative electrons embedded** in it, like plums (or currants) in a pudding
Positive charge and mass spread **evenly** through the whole atom
Total positive charge = total negative charge, so the atom is **neutral**
No nucleus and no empty space

callouts.p: The atom is a sphere of positive charge with negatively charged electrons embedded throughout it.

core.p: Around 1909, **Geiger and Marsden**, working under **Ernest Rutherford**, fired a beam of **alpha particles** (small, positively charged) at a very thin sheet of **gold foil** and recorded where they went.
bullets: Alpha source in a lead box to produce a narrow **beam**
Very **thin gold foil**: gold can be hammered extremely thin, so each alpha passes few atoms
Done in a **vacuum**, because alpha particles are absorbed by a few cm of air
A **detector** (a zinc sulfide screen that gives a tiny flash when hit) moved around the foil to count alpha particles at each angle
Prediction from the plum pudding model: the positive charge is spread out, so its force is weak and alphas should pass through with **only tiny deflections**

callouts.p: Credit is usually given for Rutherford (with Geiger and Marsden) and for the words 'alpha particles' and 'gold foil'.

core.h: Results and what each one shows
core.p: Most results matched what you might expect, but a few were astonishing: some alpha particles **bounced back**. Rutherford said it was like firing a shell at tissue paper and having it come back. Each observation leads to one conclusion.
bullets: **Most** alpha particles went **straight through**, so the atom is **mostly empty space**
**Some** were **deflected** through small angles, so the centre of the atom is **positively charged** (it repels the positive alpha)
**Very few** (about 1 in 8000) **bounced back** through more than 90 degrees, so the positive charge and **most of the mass** are concentrated in a **tiny volume** - the **nucleus**

head: Observation
Conclusion about the atom
rows: Nucleus is tiny, dense and contains most of the mass

callouts.p: Learn each observation with its conclusion as a pair: this is where most marks are.

core.h: Why the plum pudding model had to go
core.p: In the plum pudding model the positive charge is **spread thinly** across the whole atom. A spread-out charge produces only a weak force, nowhere near big enough to turn a fast, heavy alpha particle around. So **back-scattering could not be explained**, and the model was rejected.
bullets: Spread-out positive charge gives a weak repulsion
Alpha particles are fast and relatively heavy
So the plum pudding model predicts no large deflections
Only a **concentrated** positive charge with **concentrated mass** can repel an alpha back

callouts.p: The alphas bounce back because of **electrostatic repulsion** between positive charges, not because they 'hit something solid'.

core.p: Rutherford proposed the **nuclear model**: a tiny, dense, positively charged **nucleus** at the centre containing almost all the mass, with **electrons orbiting** around it at a large distance. Most of the atom is empty space.
bullets: Tiny central **nucleus**: positive, contains nearly all the mass
Electrons **orbit** the nucleus
Most of the atom is **empty space**
Explains all three scattering results
Later work showed the positive charge is carried by **protons**; Chadwick discovered the **neutron** in 1932

core.p: Rutherford's model did not explain how the electrons were arranged. Physics at the time predicted that orbiting electrons would continually **give out energy** and **spiral into the nucleus**, so atoms would collapse. It also could not explain why elements emit light only at **certain specific frequencies** (line spectra).
bullets: Orbiting electrons would lose energy and spiral inwards
Atoms would not be stable - but real atoms are
Could not explain line spectra of elements

core.p: **Niels Bohr** suggested that electrons can only orbit the nucleus in **fixed orbits** (shells) at **set distances** from the nucleus, each with a **fixed energy**. While in an orbit an electron does not lose energy, so the atom is **stable**.
bullets: Electrons occupy **fixed orbits** = **energy levels** (shells)
An electron in an orbit does **not radiate** energy
An electron moves to a **higher** orbit by **absorbing** electromagnetic radiation of exactly the right energy
It moves to a **lower** orbit by **emitting** electromagnetic radiation
Because energy levels are fixed, only certain frequencies are absorbed or emitted - this **explains line spectra**
Bohr's calculations agreed with experimental observations, so the model was accepted

callouts.p: Electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed orbits (energy levels) at specific distances from the nucleus.

core.h: Size of the atom and nucleus
core.p: The scattering experiment showed just how small the nucleus is compared with the whole atom.
bullets: Radius of an atom: about **1 x 10^-10 m**
Radius of the nucleus: about **1/100 000** of the atom's radius (around 1 x 10^-15 m)
If the atom were a football stadium, the nucleus would be a pea at the centre
Nearly all the mass is in the nucleus

core.p: A comparison table is useful for 'compare' and 'describe the differences' questions.
bullets: Key differences: where the positive charge is, where the mass is, whether there is empty space, where the electrons are

core.p: Six-mark questions often ask you to describe how and why the model changed. Tell the story in order and give the **evidence** for each change.
bullets: Start: plum pudding - positive sphere with electrons embedded (after electron discovered)
Experiment: alpha particles fired at thin gold foil in a vacuum
Results: most straight through; some deflected; few bounced back
Conclusions: empty space; positive nucleus; tiny dense nucleus with most mass
So plum pudding replaced by nuclear model
Bohr: electrons in fixed orbits / energy levels, which matched observations

callouts.p: Use 'this showed that...' and 'so...' to link each observation to its conclusion: the link is what scores.

analogy.p: Imagine firing ping-pong balls through a fog that hides what is inside a large room. If the room were filled with thin candyfloss (plum pudding), every ball would get through with barely a wobble. Instead, almost all go straight through, a few swerve, and a very rare one shoots straight back: there must be a tiny, heavy, hidden object in the middle. The analogy breaks down because the alpha particles never touch the nucleus - they are turned back by electrostatic repulsion between positive charges, not by a collision.

terms.d: A simplified representation used to explain observations and make predictions.
Thomson's model: a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it.
A tiny negatively charged particle, discovered by Thomson in 1897.
A positively charged particle equivalent to a helium nucleus; used as the 'probe' in the scattering experiment.
Experiment by Geiger and Marsden under Rutherford firing alpha particles at thin gold foil.
Very thin sheet of gold used as the target so alphas pass very few atoms.
A change in direction of an alpha particle caused by repulsion from the nucleus.
The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of the atom containing most of its mass.
Rutherford's model: tiny positive nucleus with electrons around it and mostly empty space.
Electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed orbits (energy levels) at specific distances.
A fixed orbit with a set energy that an electron can occupy.
The force pushing like charges apart; makes the positive nucleus repel alpha particles.
A space with no air; needed so alpha particles are not absorbed before reaching the foil.
Checking of scientific work by other scientists before it is accepted.

mistakes.w: Alpha particles bounced back because they hit the electrons.
mistakes.r: They were repelled by the small, positively charged nucleus; electrons are too light to deflect alphas significantly.

mistakes.w: Most alpha particles went straight through because the foil was thin.
mistakes.r: Most went straight through because the atom is mostly empty space.

mistakes.w: The plum pudding model has a nucleus.
mistakes.r: It has no nucleus: positive charge is spread throughout the atom.

mistakes.w: Rutherford discovered the electron.
mistakes.r: Thomson discovered the electron; Rutherford's experiment led to the nucleus.

mistakes.w: Some alpha particles were deflected because the nucleus is negative.
mistakes.r: Deflection shows the nucleus is positive (it repels positive alpha particles).

mistakes.w: Bohr's model says electrons can be anywhere around the nucleus.
mistakes.r: Electrons are in fixed orbits (energy levels) at set distances from the nucleus.

mistakes.w: The experiment used beta particles.
mistakes.r: It used alpha particles fired at gold foil.

mistakes.w: Very few bounced back, which shows the nucleus is big.
mistakes.r: Very few bounced back, which shows the nucleus is very small (and dense).

exam.q: Describe the plum pudding model of the atom.
model: A sphere/ball of positive charge
With (negative) electrons embedded in it / spread throughout
exam.tip: Mention both the positive part and the electrons.

exam.q: Which particles were fired at the gold foil in Rutherford's scattering experiment?
model: Alpha particles
exam.tip: One word answer.

exam.q: Explain why the scattering experiment was carried out in a vacuum.
model: Alpha particles would be absorbed by (a few cm of) air
exam.tip: Link to alpha's short range in air.

exam.q: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. What does this show about the atom?
model: The atom is mostly empty space
exam.tip: Not 'the foil is thin'.

exam.q: A few alpha particles were deflected through very large angles. Explain what this tells us about the nucleus.
model: The nucleus is positively charged (repels the alpha particles)
The nucleus is very small / charge is concentrated
The nucleus contains most of the mass (is dense)
exam.tip: Three ideas: charge, size, mass.

exam.q: Explain why the plum pudding model could not explain the results of the alpha scattering experiment.
model: In the plum pudding model positive charge (and mass) is spread out
So it would only cause small deflections; it cannot repel alphas back
exam.tip: Contrast spread-out charge with what was seen.

exam.q: Describe how Bohr changed Rutherford's model of the atom.
model: Electrons are in fixed orbits / shells / energy levels
At specific distances from the nucleus
exam.tip: The key word is 'fixed'.

exam.q: Give two differences between the plum pudding model and the nuclear model.
model: Plum pudding: positive charge spread out; nuclear: positive charge in a tiny nucleus
Plum pudding: no empty space / mass spread out; nuclear: mostly empty space / mass concentrated in nucleus
exam.tip: Each difference must state both models.

exam.q: Suggest why scientists accepted Bohr's model.
model: It explained experimental observations (e.g. line spectra / stable atoms)
Calculations / predictions from the model agreed with experiments
exam.tip: Models are accepted when they match evidence.

exam.q: The radius of an atom is about 1 x 10^-10 m. The nucleus is about 1/100 000 of this. Calculate the radius of the nucleus.
exam.tip: Dividing by 100 000 subtracts 5 from the power.

exam.q: Describe how and why the model of the atom changed from the plum pudding model to the Bohr model. (6 marks)
model: Plum pudding: ball of positive charge with electrons embedded
Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil (Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden)
Most went straight through, so atom mostly empty space
Some deflected / a few bounced back, so a small, dense, positive nucleus
Plum pudding replaced by nuclear model with electrons orbiting a nucleus
Bohr: electrons in fixed orbits / energy levels at specific distances, which agreed with observations
exam.tip: Indicative content: give the experiment, three results with conclusions, then Bohr.

worked.q: Model answer: In the scattering experiment, about 1 in 8000 alpha particles bounced back. Explain what this result tells us and why it surprised scientists.
steps: Plum pudding predicted only tiny deflections, because spread-out positive charge gives a weak force
A large repulsive force is needed to turn a fast alpha particle round
This needs positive charge and mass concentrated in a very small region
Because so few bounced back, the chance of a head-on approach is tiny, so this region is very small
worked.ans: There is a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of the mass; it surprised scientists because the plum pudding model predicted no such large deflections.

worked.q: If a nucleus had a radius of 1 cm, roughly how big would the whole atom be?
steps: Atom radius is about 100 000 times nucleus radius
worked.ans: About 1 km in radius - showing the atom is mostly empty space.

worked.q: Applied example: A student says 'Rutherford's model was wrong, so scientists wasted their time'. Evaluate this statement.
steps: Rutherford's model correctly explained the alpha scattering evidence (empty space, nucleus)
It could not explain stable electron orbits or line spectra
Bohr built on it, keeping the nucleus and adding fixed energy levels
worked.ans: The statement is wrong: each model was the best explanation of the evidence at the time, and new models build on old ones as new evidence appears.

phy_edx.5.10.summary: How long a radioactive material stays dangerous depends on its **half-life**. A material with a **short half-life** has a **high activity** at first, so it is very hazardous for a short time, but its activity falls quickly and soon becomes safe; a material with a **long half-life** has a lower activity but stays radioactive for a **very long time**. This explains why medical tracers use short half-life isotopes, why long half-life nuclear waste must be stored safely for thousands of years, and how the hazard of contamination depends on half-life as well as on the type of radiation.

core.p: Triple students must **explain how the dangers of ionising radiation depend on half-life** and relate this to the hazards of contamination and irradiation. The key idea is that half-life tells you **how quickly the activity falls**, and so **how long** a material remains dangerous.
bullets: **Short half-life**: activity drops quickly, so the hazard lasts a short time.
**Long half-life**: activity drops slowly, so the hazard lasts a long time.
For the same number of radioactive nuclei, a short half-life means **more decays per second** (higher activity) at the start.
The danger also depends on the **type of radiation** (alpha, beta, gamma) and whether it is **inside or outside** the body.

callouts.p: The time taken for half of the undecayed nuclei in a sample to decay, or the time taken for the activity of a source to halve.

core.p: Activity is the number of decays per second, measured in **becquerels (Bq)**. Every half-life the activity **halves**. After n half-lives the activity is the starting activity multiplied by (1/2) to the power n.
bullets: After 1 half-life: 1/2 left; after 2: 1/4; after 3: 1/8; after 4: 1/16; after 5: 1/32.
After about **10 half-lives** the activity is about 1/1000 (1/1024) of the start, often taken as negligible.
So a substance with a half-life of 6 hours is almost gone in about 2 to 3 days, but one with a half-life of 24 000 years needs about 240 000 years.
Activity never quite reaches zero, but it can fall below **background** level.

callouts.p: Time to become 'safe' is roughly a fixed number of half-lives, so the time a material is dangerous is proportional to its half-life.

fig.cap: Each half-life the activity halves: after 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 half-lives the fraction of the original activity left is 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16 and 1/32.

core.h: Why a short half-life means a high activity
core.p: Imagine two samples with the **same number of radioactive nuclei**. In the sample with a short half-life, each nucleus is much more likely to decay in any second, so many more decay each second. The **activity is high**, but the nuclei are used up quickly.
bullets: Short half-life: **intense** radiation for a short time.
Long half-life: **weak** radiation, but it carries on for a very long time.
The total number of decays eventually is the same (one per nucleus); half-life controls how they are **spread out in time**.
So a short half-life source can give a **large dose quickly** if you are near it.

fig.cap: Two samples with the same number of nuclei. The short half-life sample (red) starts with a much higher activity but falls quickly. The long half-life sample (blue) starts lower but is still active long after the red one has almost stopped.

core.p: Neither short nor long half-life is simply 'safe'. Each brings a different kind of danger, and exam questions want you to explain both sides.

head: Feature
Short half-life
Long half-life
rows: Very long time (years to millions of years)
Large dose in a short time if exposed
Exposure continues for a long time; storage and leaking
Keeps irradiating body tissue for years
Medical tracers and PET (danger soon over)
Long-lasting sources, e.g. smoke alarms, dating

bullets: A source with a **moderate** half-life (years to decades, e.g. caesium-137, about 30 years) can be especially troublesome: active enough to be harmful and long-lived enough to stay around.

core.p: If radioactive material gets **into** the body, the person is exposed for as long as the material stays there **and** keeps decaying. Half-life is therefore crucial when judging the hazard of contamination.
bullets: A **long half-life** contaminant (such as plutonium-239, an alpha emitter) can stay in the body for years, damaging cells all the time, so it is very dangerous.
A **short half-life** contaminant soon decays, so the total exposure is limited.
Contaminated land or water with long half-life isotopes stays unusable for a long time.
The body may also remove some material naturally, but you cannot rely on that for exam answers.

callouts.p: Always combine half-life with the type of radiation and where the source is. An alpha emitter with a long half-life inside the body is the worst case: strongly ionising AND long-lasting.

core.p: For a source **outside** the body, the dose depends on its **activity** and how long you are exposed. Half-life matters less because you can move away, shield it or remove it.
bullets: A short half-life source is most intense when fresh, so handling it soon after it is made needs extra care.
A long half-life source keeps the same activity for years, so it needs careful **long-term storage** and labelling.
Sealed sources in schools (e.g. cobalt-60 about 5 years, strontium-90 about 29 years) are chosen to last for many years of lessons.

core.h: Medical uses: why short half-lives are chosen
core.p: Isotopes put **inside** patients (tracers) are chosen with a **short half-life** so the patient is not contaminated for long. The half-life must still be **long enough** for the test to be done.
bullets: Technetium-99m (half-life about **6 hours**) is a gamma emitter used as a medical tracer.
Fluorine-18 (half-life about **110 minutes**) is used in PET scans.
Too short: the isotope would decay before it reached the organ or before the scan was finished.
Too long: the patient would keep receiving a dose for days or weeks after the test.
Short half-life isotopes must be made **close to where they are used** and used quickly.

callouts.p: In medical questions say the half-life is 'long enough to carry out the scan but short enough that the patient's dose is low'. That phrasing picks up both marks.

core.p: Spent nuclear fuel contains isotopes with **very long half-lives** (e.g. plutonium-239, about 24 000 years). Because so many half-lives must pass before the activity becomes low, this waste stays hazardous for **thousands of years**.
bullets: It must be stored so it **cannot leak** into water or soil for that whole time.
Containers and sites must stay intact far longer than any human structure has ever lasted.
Short half-life waste (e.g. some hospital waste) can simply be **stored until it has decayed** to a safe level, then disposed of normally.
This is one of the main **disadvantages of nuclear power**.

fig.cap: High-level waste with a long half-life is set in glass, sealed in steel containers and stored deep underground in geologically stable rock, away from groundwater, because it will remain hazardous for thousands of years.

core.p: Nuclear accidents release a mixture of isotopes. Their half-lives decide how the danger changes with time.
bullets: Iodine-131 (8 days) gives the biggest hazard in the first weeks; it collects in the thyroid gland.
After a few months it has decayed, but caesium-137 (30 years) remains in the soil for decades, contaminating crops and animals.
This is why areas around serious accidents can remain restricted for many years.
Stating the half-life lets you predict how long an area or food will be unsafe.

core.p: Exam questions often combine this point with half-life calculations: work out how long a material stays hazardous, or what fraction remains after a given time.
bullets: Number of half-lives = time passed / half-life.
Fraction remaining = (1/2) to the power of the number of half-lives.
Activity remaining = starting activity x fraction remaining.
To find a time: keep halving until you reach the target activity and count the halvings, then multiply by the half-life.
Remember to compare with **background count** if a question asks when the source is no longer detectable.

core.p: Six-mark questions on this point usually ask you to compare two isotopes or decide which is more suitable or more dangerous. Structure your answer around **activity, duration, type of radiation and location**.
bullets: State which has the shorter half-life and therefore the higher activity at first.
State which stays radioactive for longer and what that means (storage, continued dose).
Bring in the type of radiation: alpha most ionising (dangerous inside), gamma most penetrating (dangerous outside).
Bring in contamination versus irradiation.
Finish with a clear judgement linked to the evidence.

analogy.p: A short half-life source is like a firework: a huge, bright burst of energy that is dangerous if you are right next to it, but it is over in seconds. A long half-life source is like a candle with the same amount of wax: much dimmer at any moment, but it keeps burning for a very long time, so it needs looking after for ages. Both eventually release the same total energy. Where it breaks down: a candle burns at a steady rate, whereas a radioactive source's activity keeps halving, and the decay of individual nuclei is random rather than a smooth burn.

terms.d: The time taken for half of the undecayed nuclei in a sample to decay, or for the activity to halve.
The number of nuclei that decay per second, measured in becquerels (Bq).
The unit of activity: one decay per second.
Activity falls quickly; high activity for a given number of nuclei; hazard lasts a short time.
Activity falls slowly; lower activity for a given number of nuclei; hazard lasts a long time.
The unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or inside an object or person.
Exposure to ionising radiation from a source outside the object; the object does not become radioactive.
The amount of ionising radiation absorbed by the body; risk of harm increases with dose.
Unwanted radioactive material; long half-life waste must be stored safely for thousands of years.
A radioactive isotope put into the body or a system so its path can be followed by detecting the radiation it emits.
Ionising radiation always present in the environment from natural and man-made sources.
It is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay; half-life describes the average behaviour of many nuclei.
Radioactive material spread into the environment after a nuclear explosion or accident.
Radioactive nuclei in a sample that have not yet decayed.

mistakes.w: A long half-life is more dangerous because it is more radioactive.
mistakes.r: A long half-life means lower activity (for the same number of nuclei) but the material stays radioactive for longer.

mistakes.w: A short half-life is safe.
mistakes.r: A short half-life gives a high activity, so it can give a large dose quickly; it becomes safe sooner.

mistakes.w: Half-life is half the time it takes for a source to stop being radioactive.
mistakes.r: Half-life is the time for the activity (or number of undecayed nuclei) to halve; a source never becomes exactly zero.

mistakes.w: After two half-lives all the nuclei have decayed.
mistakes.r: After two half-lives one quarter of the nuclei remain undecayed.

mistakes.w: Tracers have short half-lives so they decay before they reach the organ.
mistakes.r: The half-life must be long enough for the scan to be done but short enough that the patient's dose is small.

mistakes.w: Nuclear waste is dangerous because it has a short half-life.
mistakes.r: High-level waste is a problem because it contains isotopes with long half-lives that stay hazardous for thousands of years.

mistakes.w: Half-life decides how dangerous a source is, nothing else matters.
mistakes.r: Danger also depends on the type of radiation, its activity, and whether the source is inside (contamination) or outside (irradiation) the body.

mistakes.w: Heating or chemically treating waste will shorten its half-life.
mistakes.r: Half-life cannot be changed by physical or chemical conditions; waste must simply be stored until it decays.

exam.q: State what is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope.
model: Time taken for half the undecayed nuclei to decay / for the activity to halve.
exam.tip: Say 'half the nuclei' or 'activity halves'; 'half the atoms disappear' is not accepted.

exam.q: Two samples contain the same number of nuclei. Sample A has a half-life of 2 hours; sample B has a half-life of 2 years. State which has the higher activity at the start and give a reason.
model: Sample A
Shorter half-life means more nuclei decay per second / nuclei decay faster
exam.tip: Activity is decays per second, so short half-life means high activity.

exam.q: Explain why technetium-99m, with a half-life of 6 hours, is suitable for use as a medical tracer.
model: Half-life long enough for the scan/test to be carried out
Short enough that it decays quickly so the patient receives only a small dose
exam.tip: Mention both 'long enough' and 'short enough'.

exam.q: Explain why waste containing plutonium-239 (half-life 24 000 years) must be stored for a very long time.
model: Long half-life so activity falls very slowly
So it remains hazardous/radioactive for thousands of years
exam.tip: Link long half-life to time remaining dangerous.

exam.q: A sample of radioactive waste has an activity of 3200 Bq and a half-life of 30 years. Calculate how long it takes for the activity to fall to 200 Bq.
model: 4 half-lives
4 x 30 = 120 years
exam.tip: Show the halving chain so you get method marks even if you slip.

exam.q: Hospital waste contaminated with an isotope of half-life 8 days is stored on site before disposal. Suggest why it is stored rather than disposed of straight away.
model: The short half-life means activity falls quickly
After some weeks/about 10 half-lives the activity is low enough to dispose of safely
exam.tip: Storing short half-life waste until it decays is a standard answer.

exam.q: Explain why an alpha emitter with a long half-life is particularly dangerous if it is breathed in.
model: Breathing in is contamination / source is inside the body next to cells
Alpha is strongly ionising so damages nearby cells / DNA
Long half-life means it keeps decaying for a long time
So cells are exposed for a long time, increasing the risk of cancer/mutation
exam.tip: Combine radiation type and half-life; each earns separate marks.

exam.q: After a nuclear accident, iodine-131 (half-life 8 days) and caesium-137 (half-life 30 years) were released. Explain how the main hazard changes over the following years.
model: At first iodine-131 is the main hazard because its short half-life gives a high activity
Iodine-131 decays to a very low level within a few months
Caesium-137 has a long half-life so remains in the environment for decades
So long-term contamination of land/food is due to caesium-137
exam.tip: Talk about early hazard and long-term hazard separately.

exam.q: Compare the dangers of radioactive isotopes with short half-lives and long half-lives. Refer to contamination and irradiation in your answer.
model: Short half-life: high activity for a given number of nuclei
Can give a large dose quickly if irradiated or contaminated
But activity falls quickly so the hazard does not last long
Long half-life: lower activity but remains radioactive for a very long time
If it contaminates a person, it keeps irradiating tissue for years
Long half-life waste needs secure storage for thousands of years; danger also depends on type of radiation (alpha worst inside)
exam.tip: Balance both sides and use 'so' to link each property to its consequence.

exam.q: A school source of strontium-90 has a half-life of 29 years. Suggest one reason why a source with this half-life is chosen for school use.
model: Activity stays almost constant over many years so it can be used for a long time / results are consistent.
exam.tip: For long-lasting sources the benefit is that they do not need replacing.

worked.q: A tracer of technetium-99m (half-life 6 hours) is injected with an activity of 800 MBq. What is its activity after 24 hours, and what fraction is left?
steps: Number of half-lives = 24 / 6 = 4.
Fraction remaining = (1/2)^4 = 1/16.
Activity = 800 / 16 = 50 MBq.
So after a day the activity is only 1/16 of the start: the patient's dose falls quickly.
worked.ans: 50 MBq, which is 1/16 of the original activity.

worked.q: Waste contains caesium-137 (half-life 30 years). How long until its activity falls to about 1/1000 of its original value?
steps: So about 10 half-lives are needed.
Time = 10 x 30 = 300 years.
Compare: technetium-99m would take only 10 x 6 = 60 hours.
worked.ans: About 300 years: the time a material stays hazardous is proportional to its half-life.

worked.q: Model answer: Isotope X (alpha, half-life 2 minutes) and isotope Y (alpha, half-life 1000 years) both contaminate a worker's lungs. Which is more harmful in the long term?
steps: Both are alpha emitters inside the body, so both are strongly ionising next to living cells.
X has a very short half-life, so its activity is high at first but almost all of it decays within about 20 minutes.
Y has a very long half-life, so its activity hardly falls during the worker's lifetime.
Y therefore keeps damaging lung cells for many years, increasing the risk of mutation and cancer.
worked.ans: Y is more harmful in the long term because its long half-life means the lungs are irradiated continuously for the rest of the worker's life.

phy_edx.5.11.summary: Radioactive isotopes are used in medicine both to **treat** disease and to **diagnose** it. In **radiotherapy** ionising radiation kills cancer cells, either from a beam **outside the body** (usually gamma rays aimed from several directions) or from a source placed **inside the body** next to the tumour. In **diagnosis**, **tracers** that emit gamma rays are put into the body and detected outside it, and **PET scanners** detect pairs of gamma rays produced when **positrons** annihilate with electrons; PET isotopes have such **short half-lives** that they must be **produced near the hospital**.

core.p: The spec asks you to (a) **compare and contrast treating tumours** with radiation applied **internally** or **externally**, (b) **explain uses of radioactive substances in diagnosis**, including **tracers** and **PET scanners**, and (c) **explain why PET isotopes must be produced nearby**. Every use depends on choosing the right **type of radiation** and the right **half-life**.
bullets: **Treatment** (radiotherapy) wants radiation to be **absorbed** by and **kill** cancer cells.
**Diagnosis** wants radiation to **escape** the body so it can be **detected**, while doing as little damage as possible.
So treatment often uses ionising radiation absorbed in the tumour; diagnosis uses **gamma** (penetrating, weakly ionising).
Both rely on balancing **benefit** against the **risk** of damaging healthy cells.

core.p: Ionising radiation damages the **DNA** of cells it passes through. A large enough dose **kills** cells. Cancer cells divide rapidly and are less able to repair DNA damage, so a carefully targeted dose kills the tumour while healthy tissue can recover.
bullets: The aim is a **high dose to the tumour** and a **low dose to healthy tissue**.
Treatment is usually given in many small doses (sessions) so healthy cells can recover between them.
Side effects (tiredness, hair loss, skin soreness, sickness) come from damage to healthy cells.
Radiotherapy may destroy a tumour completely or shrink it.

core.p: In **external** radiotherapy, a beam of high-energy **gamma rays** (or X-rays) from outside the body is aimed at the tumour. The beam has to pass through healthy tissue to reach the tumour, so it is aimed from **several different directions** (or the source **rotates** around the patient), with the tumour at the centre.
bullets: Gamma is used because it is **penetrating** enough to reach deep tumours.
Every beam passes through the tumour, so the tumour receives a **large total dose**.
Each piece of healthy tissue is crossed by only **one** beam, so it receives a **much smaller dose**.
The beam can be shaped to the outline of the tumour; lead shields protect other parts of the body.
Sources include cobalt-60 (gamma) or a linear accelerator producing high-energy X-rays.
The patient is **irradiated, not contaminated**, so they are **not radioactive** afterwards.

core.p: In **internal** radiotherapy, a radioactive source is put **inside the body, in or next to the tumour**. This can be a small **sealed implant** (a 'seed' or wire) placed in the tumour, or a radioactive substance that is swallowed or injected and naturally collects in the target organ.
bullets: Often uses a **beta** emitter (or sometimes alpha): **short range** so the radiation is absorbed within the tumour and does not travel far into healthy tissue.
**Iodine-131** is swallowed to treat **thyroid cancer** (or an overactive thyroid): the thyroid absorbs iodine, so the isotope concentrates there; it emits beta particles that destroy thyroid tissue.
Sealed implants are used for e.g. prostate or cervical cancer, then removed or left to decay.
The patient is **contaminated/contains a source** for a while, so may need to avoid close contact with others (especially children and pregnant women) until the activity falls.
A suitable **half-life** is chosen so the source is active long enough to treat the tumour but then decays.

core.h: Internal versus external: compare and contrast
core.p: This is a favourite 6-mark question. Similarities: both use **ionising radiation** to **kill cancer cells** by damaging DNA, and both carry the risk of damaging healthy cells. The differences are about **type of radiation, where the source is, and who is exposed**.

head: Feature
External
Internal
rows: Inside the body, in or near the tumour
Must penetrate tissue to reach the tumour
Strongly ionising and absorbed within the tumour
Beam passes through it; reduced by using several directions
Little damage, because radiation has a short range
Yes, for a while: contains the source
Staff must be shielded during treatment
Visitors and staff may need to keep away for a time

Small, localised tumours; organs that absorb the isotope (thyroid)
More healthy tissue exposed; many sessions
May need surgery to insert; source must be handled and disposed of

callouts.p: 'Compare' means say what is the same AND what is different. Start with a similarity (both kill cancer cells by ionising/damaging DNA), then give paired differences: 'External uses gamma because...; whereas internal uses beta because...'.

core.p: A **tracer** is a radioactive isotope (often attached to a chemical the body uses) that is **injected, swallowed or breathed in**. It travels around the body and collects in particular organs. A **gamma camera** outside the body detects the radiation, building an image of where the tracer has gone and showing how well an organ is working.
bullets: The tracer must emit **gamma** rays: they are **penetrating**, so they **pass out of the body** to the detector.
Gamma is **weakly ionising**, so it does less damage to cells on the way out.
Alpha would be useless (absorbed in the body, cannot be detected) and **very dangerous** inside the body.
Beta would mostly be absorbed in the body and would be more ionising than gamma.
The tracer must have a **short half-life** (hours), long enough for the test but short enough to limit the dose.
It should also be **non-toxic** and decay into a stable or low-hazard product.
Common example: **technetium-99m** (gamma emitter, half-life about 6 hours).
Iodine-123 can be used to check thyroid function, because the thyroid absorbs iodine.

callouts.p: Gamma emitter (to escape and be detected, weakly ionising), short half-life (low dose), non-toxic. Three properties, three marks.

core.p: Because tracers follow the body's own chemistry, doctors can see **how an organ is working**, not just its shape. Areas that absorb more tracer appear brighter; blocked or inactive areas appear darker.
bullets: Find **blockages** in blood vessels or kidneys (the tracer does not get through).
Check **thyroid** activity using radioactive iodine.
Locate **tumours** or areas of unusual activity in bones and organs.
Measure blood flow in the heart or brain.
The same idea is used in industry to find leaks in underground pipes.

core.p: PET stands for **positron emission tomography**. A positron is the antiparticle of the electron: same mass, but **positive charge (+1)**. It is emitted in **beta-plus decay**, when a proton in the nucleus changes into a neutron and a positron.
bullets: The emitted positron travels only a very short distance (about a millimetre) in tissue.
It then meets an **electron** and they **annihilate**: both particles are destroyed.
Their mass is converted into energy as **two gamma rays** emitted in **opposite directions** (180 degrees apart).
Because the two gamma rays travel in opposite directions, detecting both shows the line along which the annihilation happened.

callouts.p: When a particle meets its antiparticle (a positron meets an electron), both are destroyed and their mass is converted into energy in the form of two gamma rays travelling in opposite directions.

core.p: The patient is injected with a substance labelled with a **positron-emitting isotope**, most often **fluorine-18** attached to glucose (**FDG**). Active cells use more glucose, so the tracer collects in very active tissue such as **tumours**, the brain or the heart. The patient lies inside a **ring of gamma-ray detectors**.
bullets: Fluorine-18 decays by beta-plus decay, emitting positrons.
Each positron annihilates with an electron, producing **two gamma rays in opposite directions**.
Two detectors on opposite sides of the ring detect the gamma rays **at the same time**.
The computer draws a line between the two detectors: the annihilation happened somewhere along it.
Many thousands of these lines build up a **3D image** of where the tracer is concentrated.
Gamma rays are used because they **penetrate** out of the body; the positrons themselves never leave the body.

core.h: Why PET isotopes must be produced nearby
core.p: Positron-emitting isotopes used in PET have **very short half-lives**: fluorine-18 is about **110 minutes**, and others such as carbon-11, nitrogen-13 and oxygen-15 last only minutes. They are made in a **cyclotron** (a particle accelerator).
bullets: With such short half-lives, the activity **falls rapidly** after production.
If made far away, most of the isotope would **decay during transport**, leaving too little activity for a scan.
So they must be **produced on site or nearby** and used quickly.
The short half-life is also a benefit: the patient's dose is small because the activity falls quickly after the scan.
This makes PET **expensive** and only available in some hospitals.

callouts.p: 'Short half-life, so the activity would fall too much / most would decay before it reached the hospital; so it must be produced nearby.'
Say the isotope decays and its activity falls. Avoid vague words like 'it would wear off'.

core.p: Almost every medical question can be answered by asking two things: **what type of radiation** and **what half-life**?

head: Use
Radiation needed
Half-life needed
Example
rows: Long enough for a long-lasting source

bullets: Alpha is never used as a tracer: it cannot leave the body and is the most damaging inside it.

core.p: Every medical use of radiation carries a risk of causing **mutations and cancer**, so the **benefit must outweigh the risk**, and doses are kept as low as possible.
bullets: Radiographers leave the room or stand behind **lead screens**; they wear **dosimeter badges**.
Isotopes are handled with **tongs/syringe shields** and stored in lead containers.
Patients with internal sources or tracers may be asked to avoid close contact with others for a short time.
Pregnant women are usually not scanned, because a developing foetus is especially sensitive.
Radioactive hospital waste with short half-lives is stored until it has decayed.

analogy.p: External radiotherapy is like several dim spotlights shone from different directions at an actor on a dark stage: where they all cross, the actor is brightly lit, but each part of the stage they pass over is only dimly lit by one beam. Internal radiotherapy is like putting a small lamp right inside a box you want to light: the light hardly escapes, so the surroundings stay dark. A tracer is like a glowing marker swallowed by a fish so you can follow it from above the water. Where it breaks down: light does not damage the stage, but radiation damages every cell it ionises, and radiation decays away over time rather than being switched off.

terms.d: Treatment of cancer using ionising radiation to kill cancer cells.
Radiotherapy in which a beam of gamma rays (or X-rays) from outside the body is aimed at the tumour, usually from several directions.
Radiotherapy in which a radioactive source is placed in or near the tumour inside the body, or swallowed/injected so it collects there.
A mass of cells that have divided uncontrollably.
A radioactive isotope put into the body whose radiation is detected outside the body to show where it goes.
A detector placed outside the body that detects gamma rays from a tracer to form an image.
A gamma-emitting isotope with a half-life of about 6 hours, widely used as a medical tracer.
The antiparticle of the electron: same mass, charge +1; emitted in beta-plus decay.
Decay in which a proton in the nucleus changes into a neutron and a positron is emitted.
A positron and an electron meet and are destroyed, their mass converted into two gamma rays travelling in opposite directions.
Positron emission tomography: detects pairs of gamma rays from positron annihilation to make a 3D image of where a tracer collects.
A positron emitter with a half-life of about 110 minutes, attached to glucose for PET scans.
A particle accelerator used to produce short half-life isotopes for PET, usually at or near the hospital.
The time taken for half the undecayed nuclei in a sample to decay, or for the activity to halve.
A beta and gamma emitter (half-life about 8 days) taken up by the thyroid, used to treat thyroid cancer.
The amount of ionising radiation absorbed by the body; the risk of harm increases with dose.

mistakes.w: Tracers use alpha because it is the most ionising so it is easy to detect.
mistakes.r: Tracers use gamma: it penetrates out of the body to be detected and is weakly ionising so does least damage; alpha cannot escape the body.

mistakes.w: A tracer should have a long half-life so it lasts.
mistakes.r: A short half-life: long enough for the scan, short enough that the patient's dose is small.

mistakes.w: In external radiotherapy the beam only hits the tumour.
mistakes.r: The beam passes through healthy tissue too; aiming from several directions keeps the dose to healthy tissue low while the tumour gets a high total dose.

mistakes.w: The patient is radioactive after external radiotherapy.
mistakes.r: External radiotherapy irradiates the patient; they do not become radioactive. Only internal sources make the patient radioactive for a while.

mistakes.w: In PET the positrons are detected.
mistakes.r: Positrons annihilate with electrons inside the body; the two gamma rays produced are what the detectors pick up.

mistakes.w: Annihilation produces one gamma ray.
mistakes.r: Two gamma rays are produced, travelling in opposite directions.

mistakes.w: PET isotopes are made nearby because they are dangerous to transport.
mistakes.r: They have very short half-lives, so most would decay during transport and there would not be enough activity left for the scan.

mistakes.w: Internal radiotherapy uses gamma rays so they reach the tumour.
mistakes.r: Internal sources are already at the tumour, so short-range beta (or alpha) is used so the radiation is absorbed by the tumour, not healthy tissue.

mistakes.w: Radiotherapy kills only cancer cells.
mistakes.r: It also damages healthy cells, which causes side effects; the dose to healthy cells is kept as low as possible.

exam.q: State the type of radiation that should be emitted by a medical tracer.
model: Gamma.
exam.tip: One word; no explanation needed for 1 mark.

exam.q: Explain why a medical tracer should emit gamma radiation.
model: Gamma is penetrating so it passes out of the body and can be detected
Gamma is weakly ionising so causes less damage to cells
exam.tip: One mark for detection, one for safety.

exam.q: Explain why technetium-99m, with a half-life of 6 hours, is a suitable tracer.
model: Half-life long enough for the scan to be carried out
Short enough that activity falls quickly so the patient receives a low dose
exam.tip: Always give both sides of the half-life argument.

exam.q: Describe what happens when a positron meets an electron.
model: They annihilate / both are destroyed
Two gamma rays are produced travelling in opposite directions
exam.tip: 'Opposite directions' is the detail that gets the second mark.

exam.q: Explain why the isotopes used in PET scanners must be produced close to the hospital.
model: They have a very short half-life
So they would decay / activity would fall too much during transport
exam.tip: Link short half-life directly to decaying in transit.

exam.q: In external radiotherapy, gamma rays are directed at a tumour from several different directions. Explain why.
model: The tumour is where all beams meet, so it receives a large total dose
Each region of healthy tissue is crossed by only one beam
So healthy tissue receives a smaller dose / less damage
exam.tip: Contrast dose to tumour with dose to healthy tissue.

exam.q: Iodine-131 is swallowed to treat thyroid cancer. It emits beta particles. Explain why this treatment targets the thyroid.
model: The thyroid absorbs iodine so the isotope collects there
Beta particles have a short range in tissue
So most of the energy is absorbed by thyroid cells, killing them, with little damage to other tissue
exam.tip: Mention both where the isotope goes and why its radiation stays local.

exam.q: Describe how a PET scanner produces an image of a tumour.
model: Patient injected with a positron-emitting tracer, e.g. fluorine-18 glucose, which collects in active tissue such as tumours
Positrons annihilate with electrons producing two gamma rays in opposite directions
Gamma rays detected simultaneously by detectors on opposite sides of a ring
Computer uses the lines between detectors to locate the source and build an image
exam.tip: Follow the order: injection, positron, annihilation, detection, image.

exam.q: Compare and contrast the treatment of tumours using radiation applied internally and externally.
model: Both use ionising radiation to kill cancer cells / damage DNA, and both can damage healthy cells
External: source outside the body, uses gamma (or X-rays) which can penetrate to the tumour
External: beams from several directions to reduce dose to healthy tissue; patient not radioactive afterwards
Internal: source placed in or near the tumour (implant) or swallowed/injected (e.g. iodine-131)
Internal: uses beta (short range) so radiation is absorbed by the tumour with little effect on healthy tissue
Internal: patient contains radioactive material for a time so others may be exposed; may need surgery to insert
exam.tip: Start with a similarity, then give matched differences for type of radiation, healthy tissue and risk to others.

exam.q: A hospital is choosing an isotope for diagnosis. Isotope P emits alpha with a half-life of 5 hours; Q emits gamma with a half-life of 6 hours; R emits gamma with a half-life of 30 years. Which should be chosen? Explain your answer.
model: Q
Gamma escapes the body to be detected and is weakly ionising (P's alpha would not escape and is very damaging inside)
Short half-life gives a low dose to the patient (R would remain in the body emitting radiation for years)
exam.tip: Rule out each other option with a reason.

worked.q: Fluorine-18 has a half-life of about 110 minutes. A cyclotron 330 minutes' drive away produces a sample with activity 800 MBq. What activity would reach the hospital?
steps: Number of half-lives = 330 / 110 = 3.
Fraction left = (1/2)^3 = 1/8.
Activity on arrival = 800 / 8 = 100 MBq.
Seven-eighths of the activity has been lost on the journey, which is why PET isotopes are made nearby.
worked.ans: 100 MBq, only 1/8 of the original activity.

worked.q: A hospital gives a patient 400 MBq of technetium-99m (half-life 6 hours). What is the activity in the patient after 18 hours, assuming none leaves the body?
steps: Number of half-lives = 18 / 6 = 3.
Fraction left = 1/8.
Activity = 400 / 8 = 50 MBq.
After about 2 to 3 days the activity is negligible, so the patient's dose is limited.
worked.ans: 50 MBq.

worked.q: Model answer: Why is a beta-emitting implant, rather than an external gamma beam, chosen for a small tumour deep in the prostate?
steps: An external gamma beam would have to pass through healthy tissue (bladder, bowel) to reach the tumour.
An implant is placed directly in the tumour, so the radiation starts where it is needed.
Beta particles have a short range in tissue, so they are absorbed within the tumour.
So the tumour receives a high dose while surrounding healthy organs receive very little.
Drawback: the patient contains a radioactive source for a time, so contact with others may be limited.
worked.ans: The implant concentrates the dose in the tumour because beta has a short range, protecting nearby healthy organs better than an external beam.

phy_edx.5.12.summary: Nuclear power stations use the energy released by **nuclear fission** of uranium to heat water, make steam and drive turbines and generators, just like a fossil-fuel station but without burning anything. Nuclear reactions in general (fission, fusion and radioactive decay) can all be a **source of energy**. Nuclear power produces **no carbon dioxide** while generating and gives a reliable supply from a tiny mass of fuel, but it creates **long-lived radioactive waste**, carries a small risk of serious accidents and is very **expensive to build and decommission**. Exam questions ask you to weigh these up and compare nuclear with fossil fuels and renewables.

core.h: Nuclear reactions as a source of energy
core.p: The nucleus stores a huge amount of energy in its **nuclear store**. Three kinds of nuclear reaction can transfer some of this energy: **fission**, **fusion** and **radioactive decay**. Each one releases far more energy per kilogram than any chemical reaction such as burning.
bullets: **Fission**: a large nucleus (e.g. uranium-235) splits into two smaller daughter nuclei, releasing energy and 2 or 3 neutrons. Used in nuclear power stations.
**Fusion**: two light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen) join to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy. This powers the Sun and other stars.
**Radioactive decay**: an unstable nucleus emits alpha, beta or gamma radiation; the radiation carries energy away. Decay of radioactive isotopes inside the Earth helps heat its interior.
In all three, energy is transferred from the **nuclear store** of the nuclei, mainly to the **kinetic store** of the products and then to the thermal store of the surroundings.
Nuclear energy per kg of fuel is around a million times greater than for chemical fuels, which is why so little fuel is needed.

callouts.p: Nuclear reactions, including fission, fusion and radioactive decay, can be a source of energy.

fig.cap: Fission, fusion and radioactive decay all transfer energy from the nuclear store of nuclei. Fission is used in power stations, fusion powers stars, and radioactive decay heats the inside of the Earth.

core.h: How a nuclear power station generates electricity
core.p: A nuclear power station is a **thermal power station**. The only difference from a coal or gas station is how the water is heated: by **fission in a reactor** instead of by burning fuel.
bullets: Fission of uranium-235 in the **reactor core** releases energy as kinetic energy of the fission products, which heats the fuel and the **coolant**.
The hot coolant passes through a **heat exchanger** (boiler) and heats water to make **steam**.
High-pressure steam turns a **turbine**.
The turbine drives a **generator**, which induces a voltage and produces electricity for the **National Grid**.
Steam is condensed back to water and reused; waste heat is released (e.g. to cooling towers or sea water).
Energy transfers: nuclear store -> thermal store (coolant, steam) -> kinetic store (turbine) -> transferred electrically.

callouts.p: Say the reactor heats water to make steam that turns a turbine which turns a generator. Each link in the chain is usually a separate mark.

core.h: Advantage 1: no carbon dioxide while generating
core.p: Nuclear power stations do not **burn** fuel, so they release **no carbon dioxide** or other greenhouse gases while producing electricity. This means they do not add to **global warming / climate change** during operation.
bullets: No CO2, so no contribution to the **enhanced greenhouse effect** during generation.
No sulfur dioxide, so no contribution to **acid rain**.
No smoke or soot particles, so less local air pollution and fewer breathing problems.
Some CO2 is released indirectly when mining and processing uranium and building the station from concrete and steel, but this is small per unit of electricity over the station's lifetime.
This makes nuclear a **low-carbon** energy resource, like renewables.

callouts.p: Do not say nuclear power produces no pollution. It produces no greenhouse gases while generating, but it does produce radioactive waste.

core.p: A nuclear power station can run **continuously** for long periods, day and night, in any weather. This makes it a **reliable** source of **baseload** electricity, unlike wind or solar which depend on the weather and time of day.
bullets: Output does not depend on wind, sunshine or tides.
A single station produces a very large power output (often over 1000 MW) from a small land area.
Helps a country have a **secure energy supply** and rely less on imported fossil fuels.
However, output cannot be changed quickly, so it is better for steady baseload demand than for sudden peaks.

core.h: Advantage 3: huge energy from a tiny mass of fuel
core.p: Because nuclear reactions release about a **million times more energy per kilogram** than burning, a nuclear station needs only a small mass of uranium fuel compared with the millions of tonnes of coal a similar coal station burns.
bullets: Less fuel to mine and transport.
Fuel rods last for a long time in the reactor before replacement.
Known **uranium reserves** will last many years, though uranium is still a **non-renewable** resource.
The fuel itself is relatively cheap compared with the total cost of the station.

callouts.p: Nuclear fuel is NOT renewable. Uranium is a finite resource that is being used up, even though it lasts a long time.

core.p: The products of fission are **radioactive**. Used fuel rods and contaminated materials stay dangerous for a very long time because some isotopes have **very long half-lives** (thousands of years or more).
bullets: Waste emits **ionising radiation**, which can damage cells and DNA and cause cancer.
It must be stored **securely** for thousands of years so that it does not escape into water or the environment.
High-level waste is very hot and must be cooled, often in water ponds, before long-term storage.
A common plan is **deep geological disposal**: sealing waste in containers and burying it deep underground in stable rock.
Waste must be protected from theft and from misuse in **nuclear weapons**.
Storage costs money long after the station stops producing electricity.

callouts.p: Fission products are radioactive with long half-lives, so their activity stays high for a very long time and they must be stored safely for many generations.

fig.cap: Deep geological disposal: sealed canisters of radioactive waste are placed in tunnels hundreds of metres down in stable rock, far from people and groundwater, so the rock and containers absorb the radiation while the waste decays.

core.p: Although accidents are rare, if a reactor overheats or is damaged, radioactive material can be released into the environment. This can contaminate large areas for many years.
bullets: Examples: **Chernobyl** (1986, Ukraine) and **Fukushima** (2011, Japan, after an earthquake and tsunami).
Released isotopes cause **contamination**: radioactive material is breathed in, swallowed or lands on surfaces.
People may need to be **evacuated** and land may be unusable for decades.

Modern reactors have many safety features (control rods that drop automatically, thick concrete shielding, backup cooling), so the risk is very low, but the **consequences** of an accident are severe.
Nuclear stations are also a possible target for terrorism, so they need high security.

core.p: Nuclear power stations are among the most **expensive** power stations to build, and they are also very expensive to close down safely at the end of their life.
bullets: High **building costs** and long construction times (often more than 10 years).
**Decommissioning** (dismantling the station when it closes) takes decades because the reactor and buildings are radioactive.
Ongoing costs of security, safety inspections and long-term waste storage.
Fuel costs are low, so running costs are fairly low, but total lifetime cost is high.

callouts.p: Safely shutting down and dismantling a nuclear power station at the end of its working life, including dealing with its radioactive parts.

core.p: Many people **fear** nuclear power more than the measured risk suggests, because accidents are dramatic, radiation cannot be seen and it is linked in people's minds with nuclear weapons. Scientists weigh up risk using **evidence** such as the number of deaths per unit of electricity generated.
bullets: **Perceived risk** is how dangerous people think something is; **actual risk** is measured from data.
Per unit of electricity, nuclear has caused far fewer deaths than coal, which kills many people through air pollution and mining accidents.
Public opposition can make it hard to find sites for new stations or waste stores.
Decisions about nuclear power involve **social, economic and environmental** issues as well as science.

core.h: Comparing nuclear with other energy resources
core.p: Exam questions often ask you to compare nuclear power with fossil fuels and renewables. Use a table of key features.
bullets: Nuclear and fossil fuels are both **reliable** and **non-renewable**.
Nuclear and renewables are both **low-carbon** while generating.
Only nuclear produces long-lived radioactive waste.
Renewables have no fuel cost, but are often weather-dependent.

core.p: 6 mark questions often ask you to **evaluate** or **discuss** nuclear power. You must give both sides and then reach a **justified conclusion**.
bullets: Give at least two **advantages** with reasons (e.g. no CO2 so does not contribute to climate change).
Give at least two **disadvantages** with reasons (e.g. waste has long half-life so must be stored for thousands of years).
Use **because** and **so** to link each point to its consequence.
Finish with a judgement, e.g. nuclear is a useful low-carbon baseload source if waste is stored safely.
Avoid one-word points like 'cheap' or 'dangerous' without explanation.

callouts.p: Level 3 answers in 6-mark questions are balanced, use correct terms (fission, radioactive waste, half-life, greenhouse gas) and end with a supported conclusion.
