analogy.t: A super-strength battery that leaves toxic ash
analogy.p: Nuclear fuel is like a tiny battery that can power a whole town for months without making any smoke, but when it is used up the empty casing stays poisonous for thousands of years and must be locked away. Where it breaks down: a battery stores chemical energy and can be recharged, whereas nuclear fuel releases energy from its nucleus and cannot be 'recharged', and its waste becomes less dangerous over time as it decays.

terms.d: The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus (such as uranium-235) into two smaller daughter nuclei, releasing energy and two or three neutrons.
The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, with a loss of mass and a release of energy.
The random process in which an unstable nucleus emits radiation (alpha, beta, gamma or neutrons) to become more stable.
The energy store associated with the nuclei of atoms, released by nuclear reactions.
The part of a nuclear reactor containing the fuel rods where fission takes place.
A fluid (such as water or carbon dioxide gas) that carries thermal energy from the reactor core to the heat exchanger.
The part where hot coolant transfers energy to water to produce steam.
A set of blades turned by high-pressure steam, which drives the generator.
A device that transfers energy from the kinetic store of a rotating turbine into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction.
Used fuel and contaminated materials that contain radioactive isotopes and emit ionising radiation.
The time taken for half the undecayed nuclei in a sample to decay, or for the activity to halve.
Safely shutting down and dismantling a nuclear power station at the end of its working life.
The minimum, steady level of electricity demand that is supplied continuously, often by nuclear stations.
A gas such as carbon dioxide that absorbs infrared radiation and contributes to global warming.
An energy resource that is being used up faster than it can be replaced and will eventually run out, such as uranium.
Unwanted radioactive material getting onto or into an object or person.

mistakes.w: Nuclear power produces no pollution.
mistakes.r: Nuclear power produces no carbon dioxide while generating, but it does produce radioactive waste.

mistakes.w: Nuclear fuel is renewable because it lasts a long time.
mistakes.r: Uranium is non-renewable: it is a finite resource that will run out.

mistakes.w: The reactor produces electricity directly.
mistakes.r: The reactor heats water to make steam, which turns a turbine that drives a generator.

mistakes.w: Nuclear power stations burn uranium.
mistakes.r: Uranium nuclei undergo fission; nothing is burned, so no CO2 is produced.

mistakes.w: Radioactive waste is dangerous because it is hot.
mistakes.r: It is dangerous because it emits ionising radiation, and stays radioactive for a long time because of its long half-life.

mistakes.w: Nuclear power is cheap.
mistakes.r: Fuel and running costs are low, but building and decommissioning costs are very high.

mistakes.w: Nuclear stations are unreliable because they might explode.
mistakes.r: They are reliable (run continuously, weather-independent); accidents are rare but have severe consequences.

mistakes.w: Waste can be buried anywhere.
mistakes.r: It must be sealed in containers and stored deep underground in stable geology, away from groundwater, for thousands of years.

exam.q: Name the nuclear reaction used in nuclear power stations to release energy.
model: Nuclear fission (of uranium-235 / plutonium-239)
exam.tip: Do not confuse fission (splitting) with fusion (joining).

exam.q: State three types of nuclear reaction that can be a source of energy.
model: Fission and fusion (1)
Radioactive decay (1)
exam.tip: All three must be given for full marks.

exam.q: Give one advantage of generating electricity using nuclear power rather than burning coal.
model: No carbon dioxide (greenhouse gas) produced while generating / does not contribute to global warming / no sulfur dioxide or acid rain / much more energy per kg of fuel
exam.tip: Be specific: 'better for the environment' alone will not score.

exam.q: Explain why radioactive waste from nuclear power stations must be stored for thousands of years.
model: Waste contains isotopes with a long half-life (1)
so it remains radioactive / emits ionising radiation for a long time, which is harmful to living things (1)
exam.tip: Link half-life to how long the activity stays high.

exam.q: Describe how energy from fission is used to generate electricity in a nuclear power station.
model: Fission releases energy that heats the coolant in the reactor (1)
Coolant heats water in a heat exchanger to produce steam (1)
Steam turns a turbine (1)
Turbine drives a generator which produces electricity (1)
exam.tip: Go step by step through reactor, steam, turbine, generator.

exam.q: Give two disadvantages of nuclear power.
model: Produces radioactive waste that is hard to store / must be stored for a long time (1)
Risk of accidents releasing radioactive material / high building cost / high decommissioning cost / uranium is non-renewable (1)
exam.tip: Two different ideas are needed, not two versions of 'waste'.

exam.q: Explain why nuclear power stations are described as a reliable source of electricity compared with wind turbines.
model: Nuclear stations can generate electricity continuously / on demand (1)
Wind turbines depend on the weather / wind speed, so output varies (1)
exam.tip: Comparison questions need a point about both resources.

exam.q: Suggest why the cost of electricity from a nuclear power station is high even though the fuel is cheap.
model: Building the station is very expensive / takes a long time (1)
Decommissioning and long-term waste storage are very expensive (1)
exam.tip: Separate fuel costs from total lifetime costs.

exam.q: Some people think that the risk of nuclear power is greater than it actually is. Suggest two reasons why.
model: Accidents such as Chernobyl/Fukushima are rare but dramatic and widely reported (1)
Radiation cannot be seen / is linked with nuclear weapons / long-term effects such as cancer are feared (1)
exam.tip: Talk about perceived risk versus actual risk.

exam.q: A country is deciding whether to build a new nuclear power station or a large wind farm. Evaluate the use of nuclear power for generating electricity.
model: Advantage: no CO2 released while generating, so does not contribute to climate change
Advantage: reliable, produces electricity continuously regardless of weather, unlike wind
Advantage: large energy output from small mass of fuel / small land area
Disadvantage: produces radioactive waste with long half-life that must be stored securely for thousands of years
Disadvantage: risk of accident releasing radioactive material; high building and decommissioning costs
Conclusion: a justified judgement, e.g. nuclear is a good low-carbon baseload source if waste is managed safely, while wind is renewable but intermittent
exam.tip: Balance both sides and finish with a conclusion that follows from your points.

worked.q: Model answer: Compare the environmental effects of a nuclear power station with a coal-fired power station. (4 marks)
steps: Point 1: A coal station burns coal, releasing carbon dioxide, which is a greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming.
Point 2: A nuclear station uses fission, so no carbon dioxide is released while generating.
Point 3: Coal also releases sulfur dioxide (acid rain) and particulates (air pollution); nuclear does not.
Point 4: However, nuclear produces radioactive waste with a long half-life that must be stored securely for thousands of years, and there is a small risk of accidents releasing radioactive material.
worked.ans: Coal adds CO2 and other pollutants to the atmosphere; nuclear does not, but it produces long-lived radioactive waste and carries a small risk of radioactive contamination.

worked.q: Applied example: A uranium fuel pellet of mass about 7 g can release roughly as much energy as burning 1 tonne of coal. Explain what this tells you about nuclear fuel and one consequence for a power station.
steps: Compare masses: 1 tonne = 1 000 000 g, so the coal mass is about 1 000 000 / 7, roughly 140 000 times larger.
So nuclear fuel releases vastly more energy per kilogram than chemical fuel, because nuclear reactions transfer energy from the nuclear store rather than from chemical bonds.
Consequence: a nuclear station needs only a small mass of fuel, so far less mining and transport of fuel is needed and fuel can stay in the reactor for a long time.
worked.ans: Nuclear fuel has an enormous energy per kilogram, so only a tiny mass of fuel is needed, reducing fuel transport and mining compared with coal.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain two ways a government might reduce the disadvantages of radioactive waste from nuclear power. (4 marks)
steps: Store high-level waste in cooling ponds first, because it is very hot and highly radioactive when first removed.
Then seal it in strong containers (e.g. turned into glass and put in steel canisters) so it cannot leak.
Bury it deep underground in stable rock (deep geological disposal), far from people and groundwater, so the rock absorbs the radiation.
Keep it under security and monitor it so it cannot be stolen or misused while it decays over thousands of years.
worked.ans: Seal waste in containers and store it deep underground in stable rock under secure monitoring, keeping radiation away from people while it decays.

phy_edx.5.13.summary: In **nuclear fission** a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a **slow (thermal) neutron**, becomes unstable and splits into **two smaller daughter nuclei**, releasing **two or three neutrons** and a large amount of energy as **kinetic energy of the fission products** (plus gamma radiation). The released neutrons can split more U-235 nuclei, giving a **chain reaction**. In a nuclear reactor the chain reaction is kept **controlled**: a **moderator** slows neutrons so they can be absorbed, and **control rods** absorb extra neutrons so that on average one neutron from each fission causes another. The energy heats a coolant to make steam for a turbine and generator, and the fission products are **radioactive**.

core.p: **Nuclear fission** is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei. In a reactor, fission is usually **induced**: a uranium-235 nucleus is made to split by absorbing a neutron.
bullets: Fuel: **uranium-235** (U-235); plutonium-239 can also be used.
A U-235 nucleus absorbs a **slow-moving (thermal) neutron** and becomes **uranium-236**, which is very **unstable**.
The U-236 nucleus splits into **two daughter nuclei** of roughly similar size (e.g. barium and krypton).
**Two or three neutrons** are released, along with **gamma radiation**.
Energy is released, mainly as **kinetic energy of the fission products** (daughter nuclei and neutrons).
Spontaneous fission (without a neutron) can happen but is very rare.

callouts.p: The splitting of a large nucleus, such as uranium-235, into two smaller daughter nuclei, with the release of two or three neutrons and energy.

fig.cap: Induced fission: U-235 absorbs a slow neutron, becomes unstable U-236 and splits into two daughter nuclei (here barium-141 and krypton-92) plus three neutrons. Energy is released as kinetic energy of the products.

core.p: The daughter nuclei and neutrons fly apart at very high speed, so energy is transferred from the **nuclear store** of the uranium to the **kinetic store** of the fission products. As these fast particles collide with surrounding atoms in the fuel, their kinetic energy is shared out and the fuel gets **hot** (thermal store).
bullets: Energy released per fission is huge compared with a chemical reaction (millions of times more per atom).
The total mass of the products is slightly **less** than the mass of the U-235 plus neutron; this lost mass has been converted to energy.
Gamma rays are also emitted and carry energy away.
This thermal energy is what heats the coolant in a reactor.

callouts.p: Fission releases energy in the form of kinetic energy of the fission products (daughter nuclei and neutrons).

core.p: Fission equations obey the same rules as other nuclear equations: **mass number (top)** and **atomic number (bottom)** must balance on both sides. A neutron is written with mass number 1 and atomic number 0.
bullets: Atomic numbers: 92 + 0 = 92 and 56 + 36 + 0 = 92.
Different fissions give different pairs of daughter nuclei, and 2 or 3 neutrons.
To find a missing nucleus, subtract from the totals on the left.

callouts.p: Remember to count the incoming neutron on the left AND multiply the outgoing neutrons by how many there are.

core.p: Each fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons. If these are absorbed by other U-235 nuclei, they cause more fissions, which release more neutrons, and so on. This self-sustaining process is a **chain reaction**.
bullets: Generation 1: 1 fission releases 3 neutrons.
Generation 2: 3 fissions release 9 neutrons.
Generation 3: 9 fissions release 27 neutrons, and so on.
If every neutron caused another fission, the number of fissions would grow **exponentially**, releasing energy extremely quickly.
Some neutrons escape from the fuel or are absorbed without causing fission, so not every neutron causes a fission.
Enough U-235 must be present close together for the chain reaction to keep going.

callouts.p: A process in which neutrons released by one fission go on to cause further fissions, so that the reaction keeps going by itself.

fig.cap: A chain reaction: neutrons from one fission split further U-235 nuclei, which release more neutrons. Uncontrolled, the number of fissions multiplies each generation.

core.p: In a **nuclear reactor** the chain reaction is **controlled** so that energy is released at a **steady rate**. In a **nuclear weapon** the chain reaction is **uncontrolled**, so the energy is released almost instantly in an explosion.
bullets: Controlled: on average **exactly one** neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission.
The rate of fission, and so the energy output, stays constant.
Uncontrolled: more than one neutron per fission causes further fission, so the rate grows rapidly.
Reactors are designed so they cannot explode like a bomb, but they can overheat if control fails.

fig.cap: In a reactor, control rods absorb extra neutrons so each fission leads to just one more, giving a steady output. In a bomb nothing absorbs the extra neutrons, so the reaction grows uncontrollably.

core.p: Neutrons released by fission move very **fast**. Fast neutrons are **less likely to be absorbed** by U-235 nuclei. The **moderator** slows them down so they become **thermal neutrons** that are much more likely to be absorbed and cause fission.
bullets: Moderator materials: **graphite** or **water** (sometimes heavy water).
Neutrons slow down by **colliding** with nuclei in the moderator, transferring kinetic energy to them.
The moderator surrounds the fuel rods.
Without a moderator, too few neutrons would be absorbed and the chain reaction would not be sustained in a normal reactor.
The moderator does NOT absorb neutrons; it slows them.

callouts.p: The moderator slows down neutrons so that they are more likely to be absorbed by U-235 nuclei and cause fission.

core.p: **Control rods** are made of a material such as **boron** (or cadmium) that **absorbs neutrons**. By moving them in or out of the core, operators control how many neutrons are available to cause fission.
bullets: Lowering rods further **into** the core absorbs **more** neutrons, so fewer fissions occur, the rate falls and less energy is released per second.
Raising rods **out** absorbs fewer neutrons, so the rate of fission increases.
Rods are adjusted so that, on average, **one neutron per fission** causes another fission.
In an emergency the rods are dropped fully into the core to **stop** the chain reaction (a shutdown).

callouts.p: Control rods absorb neutrons; the moderator slows neutrons. Students often swap these.

core.p: The **coolant** carries thermal energy from the hot core to the **heat exchanger**, and stops the core overheating. The **shielding** stops radiation escaping.
bullets: Coolant is pumped through the core; common coolants are **water** and **carbon dioxide gas**.
If the coolant fails the core can overheat and fuel may melt, releasing radioactive material.
The reactor is surrounded by a thick **concrete** shield (with a steel pressure vessel) to absorb **neutrons and gamma radiation**.
Shielding protects workers and the public from ionising radiation.

core.p: Energy from the controlled chain reaction is used just as in any thermal power station.
bullets: Fission heats the fuel rods, which heat the **coolant**.
Hot coolant passes through a **heat exchanger**, heating water to make **steam**.
Steam at high pressure turns a **turbine**.
The turbine turns a **generator** which produces electricity for the National Grid.
Steam is condensed and the water returned to be reheated.

callouts.p: Describe each energy transfer in order: nuclear store to thermal store of coolant, to steam, to kinetic store of turbine, then transferred electrically by the generator.

core.p: The daughter nuclei produced in fission usually have **too many neutrons** for their size, so they are **unstable** and **radioactive**. They decay, mostly by **beta-minus** emission, and many have long half-lives.
bullets: Used fuel rods are highly radioactive and very hot.
This is the source of **radioactive waste** from nuclear power.
Waste must be stored safely for a long time because some products have long half-lives.
The reactor parts can also become radioactive by absorbing neutrons.

callouts.p: The products of nuclear fission are radioactive.

core.p: This is a frequent grade 9 explanation. A fast neutron spends very little time near a U-235 nucleus, so it is unlikely to be absorbed. A slower neutron is more likely to be **captured**, making the nucleus unstable enough to split.
bullets: Fast neutron from fission -> collides with moderator nuclei -> loses kinetic energy -> becomes thermal neutron.
Thermal neutron -> absorbed by U-235 -> U-236 splits -> more fast neutrons.
The moderator therefore makes the chain reaction **possible**; the control rods make it **controlled**.

analogy.p: Imagine a room filled with set mousetraps, each holding two or three ping-pong balls. Drop one ball in and it sets off a trap, which flings out more balls that set off more traps: a chain reaction. Control rods are like people catching most of the flying balls so only one ball from each trap sets off another. The moderator is like slowing balls down so they land on traps rather than bouncing past. Where it breaks down: the traps release energy from springs, whereas fission releases energy from the nucleus and a tiny loss of mass, and real neutrons must be absorbed by the nucleus, not just hit it.

terms.d: The splitting of a large nucleus into two smaller daughter nuclei, releasing two or three neutrons and energy.
Fission caused by a nucleus absorbing a neutron.
The isotope of uranium used as fuel in most nuclear reactors; its nucleus can be split by absorbing a slow neutron.
The two smaller nuclei produced when a large nucleus undergoes fission.
A slow-moving neutron that is more likely to be absorbed by a U-235 nucleus and cause fission.
A reaction in which neutrons released by one fission cause further fissions, so it continues by itself.
A chain reaction in which, on average, one neutron from each fission causes another fission, giving a steady rate of energy release.
Material such as graphite or water that slows down neutrons by collisions so they are more likely to be absorbed by U-235.
Rods of a neutron-absorbing material such as boron, moved in and out of the core to control the rate of fission.
Fluid (e.g. water or carbon dioxide) that carries thermal energy from the reactor core to the heat exchanger.
Thick concrete and steel around the reactor that absorbs radiation and protects people.
Rods containing uranium fuel in which fission takes place.
The daughter nuclei (and neutrons) produced in fission; the daughter nuclei are radioactive.
Where hot coolant transfers thermal energy to water to make steam.

mistakes.w: The control rods slow down the neutrons.
mistakes.r: The moderator slows neutrons; control rods absorb neutrons.

mistakes.w: A neutron hits the uranium nucleus and smashes it.
mistakes.r: The U-235 nucleus absorbs a slow (thermal) neutron, becomes unstable U-236 and splits.

mistakes.w: Fission produces two neutrons and two atoms.
mistakes.r: Fission produces two daughter nuclei and two or three neutrons, plus energy (and gamma radiation).

mistakes.w: Energy is released as heat directly.
mistakes.r: Energy is released as kinetic energy of the fission products, which then heats the fuel.

mistakes.w: Pushing control rods in speeds up the reaction.
mistakes.r: Lowering control rods in absorbs more neutrons, so fewer fissions and the rate decreases.

mistakes.w: In a controlled chain reaction no neutrons cause further fission.
mistakes.r: On average exactly one neutron from each fission causes another fission.

mistakes.w: Fast neutrons are best for causing fission in a reactor.
mistakes.r: Slow (thermal) neutrons are more likely to be absorbed by U-235, which is why a moderator is used.

mistakes.w: The products of fission are safe because the uranium has been used up.
mistakes.r: The daughter nuclei are radioactive, so spent fuel is radioactive waste.

exam.q: Name the isotope commonly used as fuel in nuclear reactors.
model: Uranium-235 (accept plutonium-239)
exam.tip: Give the mass number: 'uranium' alone may not score.

exam.q: State what must happen to a uranium-235 nucleus for induced fission to take place.
model: It must absorb a (slow / thermal) neutron
exam.tip: Use the word absorb rather than hit.

exam.q: Describe what happens when a nucleus of uranium-235 undergoes fission.
model: U-235 nucleus absorbs a slow neutron (1)
becomes unstable (U-236) (1)
splits into two smaller daughter nuclei (1)
releasing 2 or 3 neutrons and energy (as kinetic energy of products / gamma) (1)
exam.tip: Four separate ideas, in order.

exam.q: Explain how a chain reaction occurs in uranium-235.
model: Each fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons (1)
these neutrons are absorbed by other U-235 nuclei, causing further fissions (1)
exam.tip: Mention the neutrons going on to cause more fission.

exam.q: State the purpose of the moderator in a nuclear reactor.
model: Slows down neutrons (1)
so they are more likely to be absorbed by U-235 nuclei / cause fission (1)
exam.tip: Say WHY slowing matters for the second mark.

exam.q: Explain how control rods are used to reduce the rate of fission in a reactor.
model: Control rods (e.g. boron) absorb neutrons (1)
Lowering them further into the core absorbs more neutrons (1)
so fewer neutrons are available to cause fission, reducing the rate (1)
exam.tip: Link direction of movement to number of neutrons absorbed.

exam.q: Complete the equation: U-235 (92) + n -> Ba-141 (56) + Kr-? (?) + 3 n
model: Atomic number 36 (92 - 56) (1)
exam.tip: Include the incoming neutron and all three outgoing neutrons.

exam.q: Explain why the waste from a nuclear reactor is radioactive.
model: The fission products / daughter nuclei are unstable (1)
so they decay, emitting ionising radiation (1)
exam.tip: Waste is radioactive because of the daughter nuclei, not because of 'leftover heat'.

exam.q: Explain the difference between the chain reaction in a nuclear reactor and in a nuclear bomb.
model: In a reactor the chain reaction is controlled: on average one neutron per fission causes another, so energy is released at a steady rate (1)
In a bomb it is uncontrolled: more than one neutron per fission causes further fission so energy is released very rapidly (1)
exam.tip: Talk about the number of neutrons causing further fission.

exam.q: Explain how a nuclear reactor produces a steady supply of energy and how this energy is used to generate electricity.
model: U-235 nuclei absorb slow neutrons and undergo fission, releasing energy and 2 or 3 neutrons
The neutrons cause further fission in a chain reaction
The moderator (graphite/water) slows neutrons so they are more likely to be absorbed
Control rods (boron) absorb neutrons so on average one neutron per fission causes another, keeping the rate steady
Energy (kinetic energy of fission products) heats the coolant, which makes steam in a heat exchanger
Steam turns a turbine which drives a generator to produce electricity
exam.tip: Cover both the reactor physics and the power station chain for Level 3.

worked.q: A U-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into strontium-94 (atomic number 38), a xenon nucleus and 2 neutrons. Find the mass number and atomic number of the xenon nucleus.
steps: Left side: mass number 235 + 1 = 236; atomic number 92 + 0 = 92.
Right side mass numbers: 94 + A + 2(1) = 236, so A = 236 - 96 = 140.
Right side atomic numbers: 38 + Z + 2(0) = 92, so Z = 92 - 38 = 54.
worked.ans: Xenon-140 with atomic number 54.

worked.q: In an uncontrolled chain reaction every fission releases 3 neutrons, and every neutron causes a new fission. Starting with one fission, how many fissions occur in the 5th generation, and why must a reactor prevent this?
steps: Generation 1: 1 fission. Each generation multiplies by 3.
Generation n has 3^(n - 1) fissions.
Generation 5: 3^4 = 81 fissions.
The number grows exponentially, so the energy release rate rises enormously in a tiny time.
A reactor uses control rods to absorb neutrons so that only one neutron per fission causes another, keeping the number of fissions per generation constant.
worked.ans: 81 fissions; control rods keep it at a steady 1 fission per generation to avoid runaway energy release.

worked.q: Model answer: A reactor operator notices the core temperature is rising. Explain what they should do and why it works. (3 marks)
steps: Lower the control rods further into the core.
Control rods (boron) absorb neutrons, so fewer neutrons are available to be absorbed by U-235.
Fewer fissions per second means less energy is released per second, so the temperature falls.
worked.ans: Lower the control rods so they absorb more neutrons, reducing the rate of fission and the energy released.

phy_edx.5.14.summary: **Nuclear fusion** is the joining of two small, light nuclei to form a **larger nucleus**, with a small **loss of mass** that is released as **energy**. Fusion of hydrogen into helium is the **energy source of stars**, including the Sun. Fusion only happens at **very high temperatures and pressures**, because positively charged nuclei **repel** each other electrostatically and must move extremely fast and collide often to get close enough to fuse. These extreme conditions are why it is so hard to build a **practical and economic fusion power station**.

core.p: In **nuclear fusion**, two light nuclei (usually isotopes of hydrogen) collide and **join together** to make one heavier nucleus. It is the opposite of fission.
bullets: Fusion creates a **larger nucleus** from **smaller nuclei**.
The mass of the new nucleus (and any particles released) is **slightly less** than the total mass of the original nuclei.
This **lost mass** is converted into **energy**, which is released.
Common example: deuterium (H-2) + tritium (H-3) -> helium-4 + neutron + energy.
Fusion of light nuclei releases even more energy per kilogram of fuel than fission.

callouts.p: The creation of larger nuclei from smaller nuclei, resulting in a loss of mass and the release of energy.

fig.cap: A deuterium nucleus (1 proton, 1 neutron) and a tritium nucleus (1 proton, 2 neutrons) fuse to form helium-4 and release a neutron. The products have slightly less mass than the reactants and the missing mass is released as energy.

core.p: Mass numbers and atomic numbers must balance, just like other nuclear equations.
bullets: H-2 (atomic number 1) + H-3 (atomic number 1) -> He-4 (atomic number 2) + n (atomic number 0)
Mass numbers: 2 + 3 = 5 and 4 + 1 = 5.
Atomic numbers: 1 + 1 = 2 and 2 + 0 = 2.
Mass numbers balance, but the actual **mass** of the products is a little **less**: that tiny difference is the energy released.

callouts.p: Mass NUMBERS balance exactly, but the actual MASS decreases slightly. The energy comes from this small loss of mass, not from mass numbers changing.

core.h: Fusion is the energy source of stars
core.p: Stars, including the Sun, are powered by **fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium** in their cores. The energy released keeps the star hot and is emitted as light and other electromagnetic radiation.
bullets: The core of the Sun is at about **15 million kelvin** and at enormous pressure.
The high pressure is caused by the **gravity** of the star's huge mass squeezing the core.
The high temperature means hydrogen nuclei move fast enough to fuse.
Energy released by fusion produces an outward pressure that balances gravity, keeping the star stable.
Stars fuse hydrogen for most of their lives; bigger stars can later fuse heavier elements too.

callouts.p: Nuclear fusion is the energy source for stars.

fig.cap: In the Sun's core, gravity creates enormous pressure and the temperature is about 15 million K, so hydrogen nuclei fuse to make helium. The energy released travels outwards and is emitted as light and heat.

core.p: Both fusion and fission release energy from the nucleus because the products have less mass than the starting materials. But they work in opposite ways.
bullets: Fission **splits** one large nucleus; fusion **joins** two small nuclei.
Fission needs a **neutron** to be absorbed; fusion needs **very high temperature and pressure**.
Fission happens in today's power stations; fusion powers stars but is not yet used for electricity.
Fission products are radioactive; the main product of fusion (helium) is not radioactive.

callouts.p: For a 'difference' question, write a comparative sentence: in fission a large nucleus splits, whereas in fusion small nuclei join.

core.h: Why fusion does not happen at low temperatures and pressures
core.p: All nuclei contain protons and so are **positively charged**. Two positive nuclei **repel** each other because of the **electrostatic force**. This repulsion gets stronger as they get closer, so at normal temperatures the nuclei never get close enough to fuse.
bullets: Nuclei must get **extremely close** for the strong nuclear force to pull them together and fuse.
At low temperature, nuclei move slowly with little kinetic energy, so the electrostatic repulsion stops and pushes them apart first.
At **very high temperature**, nuclei move very fast with lots of kinetic energy, enough to **overcome the electrostatic repulsion**.
At **very high pressure (density)**, nuclei are packed closely so **collisions are much more frequent**, so fusion happens often enough to release useful energy.
At these temperatures electrons are stripped from atoms, forming a **plasma** of nuclei and electrons.

callouts.p: Fusion needs high temperature so nuclei have enough kinetic energy to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between positively charged protons, and high pressure so collisions are frequent.

fig.cap: At low temperature, slow positive nuclei are pushed apart by electrostatic repulsion before they can fuse. At very high temperature they move fast enough to overcome the repulsion and get close enough to fuse.

core.p: Scientists have been trying to build **fusion reactors** for decades. To get fusion on Earth, the fuel must be heated to temperatures even higher than the Sun's core (over 100 million K), because we cannot create the Sun's huge gravitational pressure.
bullets: The hot **plasma** cannot touch any container, because it would melt it and the plasma would cool down.
Strong **magnetic fields** are used to hold the charged plasma away from the walls (e.g. in a ring-shaped reactor called a tokamak).
Huge amounts of energy are needed to heat the plasma and power the magnets.
Experimental reactors have produced fusion, but sustaining it for long and getting out more energy than is put in is very difficult.

fig.cap: A ring-shaped experimental fusion reactor. Magnetic fields hold the extremely hot plasma away from the walls, because no material container could survive temperatures over 100 million K.

core.p: The extreme conditions needed for fusion are exactly what make a **practical and economic** fusion power station so hard to build.
bullets: **Very high temperatures** are needed, which are hard to create and maintain.
**Very high pressures / densities** are needed, which are hard to produce on Earth.
The plasma is so hot it would destroy any material, so it must be **contained by magnetic fields**.
So far, experiments have struggled to produce **more energy out than is put in** to heat and contain the plasma.
Building and running the reactors is **extremely expensive**, so fusion is not yet economic.
Research is ongoing; no commercial fusion power station currently supplies electricity.

callouts.p: Always link the difficulty to the conditions: high temperature and pressure are needed to overcome repulsion, and these are difficult and expensive to achieve and contain.

core.h: Why fusion power is so attractive
core.p: Despite the difficulties, fusion is worth researching because it would have big advantages over fission and fossil fuels.
bullets: Fuel is plentiful: **deuterium** can be extracted from sea water.
Releases a huge amount of energy per kilogram of fuel.
**No carbon dioxide** is produced while generating.
Main product, helium, is **not radioactive**, so much less long-lived radioactive waste than fission.
No runaway chain reaction: if conditions fail, fusion simply stops.

callouts.p: Do not say fusion is already used in power stations. Current nuclear power stations all use fission.

core.p: A key idea is that energy is released because the **total mass decreases**. A tiny mass loss gives a huge energy release.
bullets: Mass before fusion > mass after fusion.
The difference in mass is released as energy (mainly kinetic energy of the products).
This is why stars slowly lose mass as they shine.
The same principle explains energy from fission.

core.p: For top-grade answers, build a chain of reasoning from charge to conditions to difficulty.
bullets: Nuclei contain protons, so they are positively charged.
Positive nuclei repel (electrostatic repulsion).
They need very high kinetic energy (very high temperature) to get close enough to fuse.
They need very high pressure/density so collisions are frequent enough.
Stars achieve this naturally due to gravity; on Earth it requires extreme heating and magnetic containment.
This makes fusion power stations technically difficult and very expensive, so not yet practical or economic.

analogy.p: Fusing two nuclei is like trying to push the north poles of two strong magnets together until they snap onto a hidden sticky patch. Roll them slowly and they just bounce apart; fling them at very high speed and they get close enough to stick, releasing energy as they do. High pressure is like cramming many magnets into a small box so collisions happen all the time. Where it breaks down: magnets repel by magnetism, whereas nuclei repel because of electrostatic forces between positive charges, and the 'sticking' in real nuclei is due to the strong nuclear force and comes with a loss of mass.

terms.d: The creation of larger nuclei from smaller nuclei, resulting in a loss of mass and the release of energy.
The splitting of a large nucleus into two smaller nuclei, releasing neutrons and energy.
An isotope of hydrogen with one proton and one neutron (H-2).
An isotope of hydrogen with one proton and two neutrons (H-3).
The force pushing apart two objects with the same type of charge, such as two positively charged nuclei.
A very hot state of matter in which electrons have been removed from atoms, leaving a mixture of nuclei and free electrons.
The small decrease in total mass during a nuclear reaction; this mass is released as energy.
The very short-range attractive force that holds protons and neutrons together in a nucleus.
A massive ball of plasma in which fusion of hydrogen into helium releases energy.
The central region of a star where temperature and pressure are high enough for fusion.
Using strong magnetic fields to hold hot plasma away from the walls of a fusion reactor.
A ring-shaped experimental fusion reactor that uses magnetic fields to contain the plasma.
The energy a particle has because it is moving; higher temperature means nuclei have more kinetic energy.
Able to produce electricity at a cost that is affordable compared with other energy resources.

mistakes.w: Fusion is when a nucleus splits.
mistakes.r: Fusion is when two small nuclei join to form a larger nucleus; splitting is fission.

mistakes.w: Fusion needs high temperature to melt the fuel.
mistakes.r: High temperature gives nuclei enough kinetic energy to overcome electrostatic repulsion between positive nuclei.

mistakes.w: Nuclei repel because they are negative / because of their electrons.
mistakes.r: Nuclei are positively charged because they contain protons, so they repel electrostatically.

mistakes.w: High pressure is needed to push the nuclei together.
mistakes.r: High pressure (density) makes collisions between nuclei more frequent so fusion happens often enough.

mistakes.w: Mass is gained in fusion because a bigger nucleus forms.
mistakes.r: Total mass decreases; the lost mass is released as energy.

mistakes.w: The Sun burns hydrogen.
mistakes.r: Hydrogen nuclei undergo nuclear fusion to form helium; nothing is burned.

mistakes.w: Fusion power stations are used in the UK today.
mistakes.r: All current nuclear power stations use fission; fusion is still experimental and not yet economic.

mistakes.w: Fusion is difficult because it is dangerous and explodes.
mistakes.r: It is difficult because the very high temperatures and pressures needed are hard to achieve and contain, and so far cost more energy than they produce.

exam.q: State the energy source of stars.
model: Nuclear fusion (of hydrogen nuclei into helium)
exam.tip: Say fusion, not burning or fission.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by nuclear fusion.
model: Two small / light nuclei join to form a larger nucleus (1)
with a loss of mass and release of energy (1)
exam.tip: Mention both joining and energy release.

exam.q: State one difference between nuclear fusion and nuclear fission.
model: Fusion joins small nuclei whereas fission splits a large nucleus (accept fission needs a neutron / fusion needs high temperature)
exam.tip: Make it clearly comparative.

exam.q: Explain why fusion releases energy.
model: The mass of the products is less than the mass of the original nuclei (1)
the lost mass is converted to / released as energy (1)
exam.tip: Talk about mass, not mass number.

exam.q: Explain why nuclear fusion does not happen at low temperatures.
model: Nuclei are positively charged (contain protons) (1)
so they repel (electrostatic repulsion) (1)
at low temperatures nuclei do not have enough kinetic energy / speed to get close enough to fuse (1)
exam.tip: Charge -> repulsion -> not enough kinetic energy.

exam.q: Explain why fusion also needs a very high pressure.
model: High pressure means nuclei are close together / high density (1)
so collisions are more frequent, making fusion more likely (1)
exam.tip: Pressure is about frequency of collisions; temperature is about energy of collisions.

exam.q: Complete the equation: H-2 (1) + H-3 (1) -> He-? (?) + n
model: Mass number 4 (1)
Atomic number 2 (1)
exam.tip: Remember the neutron has mass number 1 and atomic number 0.

exam.q: Suggest why a material container cannot be used to hold the fuel in a fusion reactor.
model: The plasma is at an extremely high temperature (over 100 million K) (1)
it would melt / damage any container (and the plasma would cool), so magnetic fields are used (1)
exam.tip: Link the temperature to the containment problem.

exam.q: Give two advantages of fusion over fission as a source of electricity.
model: Fuel (deuterium) is plentiful / from sea water (1)
Produces little long-lived radioactive waste / helium is not radioactive / no CO2 (1)
exam.tip: Avoid saying 'no waste at all'.

exam.q: Scientists have been trying to build fusion power stations for many years. Explain why it is so difficult to make a practical and economic fusion power station.
model: Nuclei are positively charged and repel each other electrostatically
Fusion therefore requires very high temperatures so nuclei have enough kinetic energy to overcome the repulsion
Very high pressure / density is needed so collisions are frequent enough
Such high temperatures are hard to create and maintain on Earth (higher than the Sun's core as Earth cannot match its gravitational pressure)
The plasma cannot touch any container so must be held by strong magnetic fields
Large amounts of energy are needed to heat and contain the plasma, so far more energy is often put in than released, making it very expensive / not yet economic
exam.tip: Start with why the conditions are needed, then why they are hard to achieve, then the cost.

worked.q: Two deuterium nuclei (H-2, atomic number 1) fuse to produce a helium nucleus and a neutron. Identify the helium isotope formed.
steps: Left: mass numbers 2 + 2 = 4; atomic numbers 1 + 1 = 2.
Right: helium (atomic number Z) + neutron (mass 1, atomic number 0).
Mass number: A + 1 = 4, so A = 3.
Atomic number: Z + 0 = 2, so Z = 2, which confirms it is helium.
worked.ans: Helium-3 (mass number 3, atomic number 2).

worked.q: Model answer: Compare how energy is produced in the Sun with how energy is produced in a nuclear power station. (4 marks)
steps: In the Sun, energy is released by nuclear fusion: hydrogen nuclei join to form helium.
In a power station, energy is released by nuclear fission: U-235 nuclei absorb neutrons and split into two daughter nuclei.
In both, the total mass of the products is less than the mass at the start, and the lost mass is released as energy.

Fusion in the Sun happens because gravity creates huge pressure and the core temperature is about 15 million K; fission happens at much lower temperatures because neutrons have no charge and are not repelled by nuclei.
worked.ans: The Sun uses fusion (joining light nuclei) at extreme temperature and pressure; a power station uses fission (splitting U-235 after neutron absorption). Both release energy from a loss of mass.

worked.q: Applied example: Explain why increasing the temperature of a hydrogen plasma increases the rate of fusion.
steps: Higher temperature means the nuclei have more kinetic energy and move faster.
Faster nuclei can get closer together before electrostatic repulsion stops them.
More nuclei have enough energy to overcome the repulsion and get close enough to fuse.
So a greater fraction of collisions result in fusion, and the rate of fusion increases.
worked.ans: At higher temperature more nuclei have enough kinetic energy to overcome electrostatic repulsion, so more collisions lead to fusion.

phy_edx.5.6.summary: Unstable nuclei become more stable by emitting radiation, and each type of emission changes the nucleus in a predictable way. In **beta-minus decay** a neutron changes into a proton and an electron, in **beta-plus decay** a proton changes into a neutron and a positron, and in **gamma emission** the nucleus simply loses energy without changing its make-up. You must be able to state how the **mass number** and **atomic number** change for alpha, beta-minus, beta-plus, gamma and neutron emission, and write **balanced nuclear equations** where both mass number and charge are conserved.

core.p: A nucleus is made of protons and neutrons. Some combinations are **unstable**: they have too many neutrons, too many protons, or too much energy. An unstable nucleus becomes more stable by emitting radiation. This happens **randomly** and **spontaneously**, so it is not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical reactions.
bullets: Too many neutrons compared with protons: the nucleus tends to undergo **beta-minus decay**.
Too many protons compared with neutrons: the nucleus tends to undergo **beta-plus (positron) decay**.
Very large, heavy nuclei (for example uranium, radium) tend to undergo **alpha decay**.
A nucleus left with excess energy after another decay often emits a **gamma ray**.
Some nuclei can also emit a single **neutron**.
The original nucleus is called the **parent**; the nucleus left behind is the **daughter**.

callouts.p: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation are all emitted from the **nucleus**, not from the electron shells. Beta particles are electrons created inside the nucleus, not orbiting electrons that escape.

core.p: Every nucleus can be written as a chemical symbol with two numbers. The top number is the **mass number A** (number of protons plus neutrons, also called the nucleon number). The bottom number is the **atomic number Z** (number of protons, also called the proton number). In plain text we write this as, for example, C-14 with A = 14 and Z = 6, or 14/6 C.
bullets: Mass number A = protons + neutrons.
Atomic number Z = number of protons, and it decides which **element** the atom is.
Number of neutrons = A minus Z.
If Z changes, the element changes. This is called **transmutation**.
For particles, the bottom number shows **charge**: electron = 0/-1 e, positron = 0/+1 e, proton = 1/1 p, neutron = 1/0 n, alpha = 4/2 He.

core.p: In **beta-minus decay** a **neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron**. The electron is ejected from the nucleus at very high speed: this fast-moving electron is the **beta-minus particle**. The proton stays in the nucleus.
bullets: Neutron becomes proton + electron (n becomes p + e-).
Number of neutrons goes **down by 1**; number of protons goes **up by 1**.
Mass number A **stays the same**, because one nucleon has just changed type.
Atomic number Z **increases by 1**, so the element moves **one place to the right** in the periodic table.
Charge is conserved: neutron (0) becomes proton (+1) plus electron (-1), and 0 = +1 + (-1).
Example: carbon-14 decays to nitrogen-14: 14/6 C becomes 14/7 N + 0/-1 e.
Beta-minus decay happens in nuclei with **too many neutrons**.

callouts.p: A neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron; the electron is emitted as a high-speed beta-minus particle.

fig.cap: Beta-minus decay: inside the nucleus a neutron (grey) turns into a proton (red), which stays, and an electron, which is emitted at high speed as the beta-minus particle. A stays the same and Z rises by 1.

core.p: In **beta-plus decay** a **proton in the nucleus changes into a neutron and a positron**. The **positron** is the antiparticle of the electron: it has the same mass as an electron but a **positive charge (+1)**. The positron is emitted from the nucleus at high speed; the neutron stays.
bullets: Proton becomes neutron + positron (p becomes n + e+).
Number of protons goes **down by 1**; number of neutrons goes **up by 1**.
Mass number A **stays the same**.
Atomic number Z **decreases by 1**, so the element moves **one place to the left** in the periodic table.
Charge is conserved: proton (+1) becomes neutron (0) plus positron (+1).
Example: fluorine-18 (used in PET scans) decays to oxygen-18: 18/9 F becomes 18/8 O + 0/+1 e.
Beta-plus decay happens in nuclei with **too many protons**.

callouts.p: A proton in the nucleus changes into a neutron and a positron; the positron is emitted as a high-speed beta-plus particle.

callouts.t: Do not mix up the signs
callouts.p: Beta-minus: Z goes UP by 1 (gain a proton). Beta-plus: Z goes DOWN by 1 (lose a proton). The sign of the particle is the opposite of the change in Z.

core.p: A **gamma ray** is a high-frequency **electromagnetic wave**, not a particle with mass or charge. After an alpha or beta decay the nucleus is often left in an **excited state** with too much energy. It loses this energy by emitting a gamma ray as the nucleons **rearrange into a lower energy, more stable arrangement**.
bullets: Gamma emission changes **neither** the mass number nor the atomic number.
The **element stays the same**; the number of protons and neutrons is unchanged.
The nucleus simply **loses energy**: it goes from an excited (higher energy) state to a lower energy state.
Gamma rays usually follow alpha or beta decay, because those decays often leave the daughter nucleus excited.
In an equation gamma is written as 0/0 gamma, and it does not affect the balance of A or Z.

callouts.p: Only the **energy** of the nucleus decreases. Composition (protons and neutrons) stays the same, so A and Z are unchanged.

core.p: For a complete answer on how decays change a nucleus you must also know the other two emissions. An **alpha particle** is **2 protons and 2 neutrons** (a helium nucleus). In **neutron emission** a single neutron leaves the nucleus.
bullets: Alpha: mass number **decreases by 4**, atomic number **decreases by 2**. A new element, two places left in the periodic table.
Example: 226/88 Ra becomes 222/86 Rn + 4/2 He.
Neutron emission: mass number **decreases by 1**, atomic number **unchanged**.
Because Z does not change in neutron emission, the element stays the same; you get a **lighter isotope** of the same element.
Example: 5/2 He becomes 4/2 He + 1/0 n.

core.h: Summary table: effect of each decay
core.p: This table is the single most examined fact for this spec point. Learn it so you can fill in any row from memory.
bullets: Only alpha changes A by more than 1.
Beta-minus and beta-plus leave A unchanged but change Z by one.
Gamma changes nothing except energy.
Neutron emission changes A but not Z, so it makes an isotope of the same element.

fig.cap: Moving on a chart of neutron number N against proton number Z: alpha moves 2 down and 2 left, beta-minus moves 1 right and 1 down, beta-plus moves 1 left and 1 up, and neutron emission moves 1 down. Gamma does not move the nucleus at all.

core.p: A nuclear equation shows the parent nucleus on the left and the daughter nucleus plus emitted radiation on the right. It must be **balanced for mass number and for charge (atomic number)**. This is because **nucleons are conserved** and **charge is conserved** in every nuclear decay.
bullets: Rule 1: **total of the top numbers (A) on the left = total of the top numbers on the right**.
Rule 2: **total of the bottom numbers (Z or charge) on the left = total of the bottom numbers on the right**.
Step 1: write the parent nucleus with its A and Z.
Step 2: write the emitted particle with its correct symbol, for example 4/2 He or 0/-1 e.
Step 3: find the daughter's A by subtraction, then its Z by subtraction.
Step 4: use Z to identify the element from the periodic table.
Step 5: check both rows add up.
For beta-minus remember subtracting -1 means Z goes **up**: Z(daughter) = Z(parent) - (-1) = Z(parent) + 1.

callouts.p: In a 'complete the equation' question, examiners give a mark for each correct number. Writing the sums (e.g. 238 = 234 + 4 and 92 = 90 + 2) helps you catch errors.

fig.cap: A balanced alpha decay equation for uranium-238. The mass numbers balance (238 = 234 + 4) and the atomic numbers balance (92 = 90 + 2), so the daughter must be thorium (Z = 90).

core.h: Worked equations for each decay type
core.p: Practise writing one equation for each decay so the pattern becomes automatic.
bullets: Beta-plus: 11/6 C becomes 11/5 B + 0/+1 e (check: 11 = 11 + 0; 6 = 5 + 1).
Gamma: 60/28 Ni (excited) becomes 60/28 Ni + 0/0 gamma (nothing changes but energy).
Neutron: 9/4 Be (excited) can lose a neutron to form 8/4 Be + 1/0 n (check: 9 = 8 + 1; 4 = 4 + 0).

core.p: A daughter nucleus may itself be unstable and decay again. A series of decays is called a **decay chain**. Exam questions may give you several steps and ask you to identify each emission from the change in A and Z, or to find the final nucleus.
bullets: Look at the change in A: a drop of 4 means alpha; no change means beta or gamma; a drop of 1 means neutron.
Then look at Z: -2 is alpha, +1 is beta-minus, -1 is beta-plus, 0 with no change in A is gamma.
Example: an alpha decay followed by two beta-minus decays gives total change A -4 and Z -2 + 1 + 1 = 0. The final nucleus is an **isotope of the original element**, 4 lighter.
Uranium-238 decays through a long chain of alpha and beta-minus decays to stable lead-206.

callouts.p: If asked what decay turned X into Y, subtract: change in A and change in Z identify the particle uniquely.

core.h: Why the changes happen: linking ideas
core.p: Every rule above comes from two conservation laws plus knowing what each particle is made of. If you understand that, you never need to memorise the table blindly.
bullets: **Nucleon number is conserved**: protons and neutrons can change into each other but are not destroyed, so A stays constant in beta decay.
**Charge is conserved**: when a neutral neutron becomes a positive proton, a negative electron must be made to keep total charge at zero.
When a positive proton becomes a neutral neutron, a positive positron must be made.
Electrons and positrons have a mass number of 0 because their mass is tiny compared with a nucleon.
Gamma rays have no mass and no charge, so they cannot change A or Z; they carry away **energy** only.
Changing the number of protons changes the element, which is why alpha and beta decay cause **transmutation**.

analogy.p: Think of the nucleus as a squad of players wearing red (proton) or grey (neutron) shirts. Mass number is the total number of players; atomic number is the number in red. In beta-minus decay a grey player swaps to a red shirt and throws a small negative token (electron) out of the stadium: the squad size is the same but there is one more red. In beta-plus a red player swaps to grey and throws out a positive token (positron). In alpha decay two reds and two greys leave together. In gamma emission nobody leaves or changes shirt; the team just calms down and releases energy as a cheer. Where it breaks down: real nucleons are not simply relabelled; the electron or positron is genuinely created at the moment of decay and did not exist inside the nucleus beforehand, and the process is random, not chosen.

terms.d: The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus.
The number of protons in a nucleus; it determines the element.
Atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons.
A nucleus that will at some point decay by emitting radiation to become more stable.
A neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron; the electron is emitted.
A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus; mass number 0, charge -1.
A proton in the nucleus changes into a neutron and a positron; the positron is emitted.
The antiparticle of the electron: same mass as an electron but a charge of +1.
A high-frequency electromagnetic wave emitted from a nucleus that is losing energy; no mass, no charge.
A nucleus with more energy than its lowest energy state; it loses the excess by gamma emission.
Two protons and two neutrons bound together; the same as a helium nucleus, charge +2.
Emission of a single neutron from a nucleus; A decreases by 1 and Z is unchanged.
The nucleus before it decays.
The nucleus produced after a decay.
The change of one element into another when the number of protons in the nucleus changes.
An equation where the total mass number and total atomic number (charge) are the same on both sides.
A series of decays in which each daughter nucleus is itself unstable and decays again.

mistakes.w: In beta-minus decay an electron from the shells is emitted.
mistakes.r: A neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron, and that electron is emitted from the nucleus.

mistakes.w: Beta-minus decay decreases the atomic number by 1.
mistakes.r: Beta-minus increases the atomic number by 1 (a proton is gained); the mass number is unchanged.

mistakes.w: Beta decay reduces the mass number by 1 because a particle leaves.
mistakes.r: The mass number is unchanged in beta decay because the electron or positron has a mass number of 0.

mistakes.w: Gamma emission changes the element.
mistakes.r: Gamma emission changes neither A nor Z; the nucleus only loses energy, so it is the same element (and isotope).

mistakes.w: A positron is a positive proton.
mistakes.r: A positron is the antiparticle of the electron, with the mass of an electron and a charge of +1.

mistakes.w: Alpha decay: A goes down by 2 and Z goes down by 4.
mistakes.r: Alpha decay: A decreases by 4 and Z decreases by 2.

mistakes.w: Writing the beta particle as -1/0 e (numbers the wrong way round).
mistakes.r: Beta-minus is 0 on top (mass number) and -1 on the bottom (charge): 0/-1 e.

mistakes.w: The equation balances because the masses balance.
mistakes.r: Both the mass numbers AND the atomic numbers (charges) must balance on each side.

mistakes.w: Neutron emission makes a new element.
mistakes.r: Neutron emission leaves Z unchanged, so it produces a different isotope of the same element.

exam.q: Describe what happens in the nucleus during beta-minus decay.
model: A neutron changes into a proton
and an electron, which is emitted (as the beta particle)
exam.tip: Say 'in the nucleus' and name both products of the neutron.

exam.q: Describe what happens in the nucleus during beta-plus decay.
model: A proton changes into a neutron
and a positron, which is emitted
exam.tip: The particle emitted is a positron, not a proton.

exam.q: State the change in the mass number of a nucleus that emits a gamma ray.
model: No change (mass number stays the same)
exam.tip: Gamma rays have no mass.

exam.q: Explain how a nucleus changes when it emits a gamma ray.
model: The nucleus loses energy / goes to a lower energy state
The number of protons and neutrons (A and Z) does not change
exam.tip: Two separate ideas: energy decreases, composition unchanged.

exam.q: Strontium-90 (Z = 38) decays by beta-minus emission to yttrium (Y). Write the balanced nuclear equation.
model: 90/38 Sr becomes 90/39 Y + 0/-1 e
Mass number of Y = 90
Atomic number of Y = 39 and beta shown as 0/-1 e
exam.tip: Show the beta particle with its numbers; marks are lost for a bare 'e' or 'beta'.

exam.q: Polonium-210 (Z = 84) emits an alpha particle. Calculate the mass number and atomic number of the daughter nucleus.
model: Mass number = 210 - 4 = 206
Atomic number = 84 - 2 = 82
exam.tip: The daughter is lead (Pb), but only give the element if asked or if you are sure.

exam.q: A nucleus of 23/12 Mg decays to 23/11 Na. Identify the type of decay and explain your answer.
model: Beta-plus (positron) decay
Mass number has not changed
Atomic number has decreased by 1 (a proton changed into a neutron)
exam.tip: Use the change in A first, then the change in Z.

exam.q: Complete the table to show the change in mass number and atomic number for alpha, beta-minus, gamma and neutron emission.
model: Alpha: A -4, Z -2
Beta-minus: A 0, Z +1
Gamma: A 0, Z 0
Neutron: A -1, Z 0
exam.tip: One mark per correct row; learn the summary table.

exam.q: Explain why the mass number does not change in beta-minus decay even though a particle is emitted.
model: The electron has a mass number of 0 / negligible mass
One neutron becomes one proton so the total number of nucleons stays the same
exam.tip: Link to conservation of nucleon number.

exam.q: Thorium-232 (Z = 90) decays by a sequence of one alpha decay followed by two beta-minus decays. Explain what the final nucleus is, in terms of its mass number, atomic number and element.
model: Alpha decay reduces A by 4 and Z by 2
After alpha: A = 228, Z = 88 (radium)
Each beta-minus leaves A unchanged and increases Z by 1
After two beta-minus: A = 228, Z = 90
Z = 90 so the final nucleus is thorium again
It is a different isotope of thorium (thorium-228) with 4 fewer neutrons
exam.tip: Track A and Z step by step and draw a conclusion about the element and isotope.

worked.q: Carbon-14 (Z = 6) undergoes beta-minus decay. Write the balanced equation and name the daughter element.
steps: Write the parent: 14/6 C.
Beta-minus particle is 0/-1 e.
Top numbers: 14 = A + 0, so A = 14.
Bottom numbers: 6 = Z + (-1), so Z = 7.
Element with Z = 7 is nitrogen.
worked.ans: 14/6 C becomes 14/7 N + 0/-1 e; the daughter is nitrogen-14.

worked.q: Radium-226 (Z = 88) emits an alpha particle and then the daughter emits a gamma ray. Find the final nucleus.
steps: Alpha is 4/2 He.
Z: 88 - 2 = 86, which is radon.
Gamma emission changes neither A nor Z; the radon nucleus just loses energy.
Final nucleus is radon-222.
worked.ans: 226/88 Ra becomes 222/86 Rn + 4/2 He, then 222/86 Rn (excited) becomes 222/86 Rn + gamma. Final nucleus: radon-222.

worked.q: Fluorine-18 (Z = 9) decays by beta-plus emission. Write the balanced equation.
steps: Parent: 18/9 F.
Positron is 0/+1 e.
Z: 9 = Z + 1, so Z = 8, which is oxygen.
Check both rows balance.
worked.ans: 18/9 F becomes 18/8 O + 0/+1 e.

phy_edx.5.7.summary: The **activity** of a radioactive source is the rate at which its unstable nuclei decay, measured in **becquerels (Bq)**, where 1 Bq is one decay per second. Radioactive decay is **random**, so we cannot predict when any one nucleus will decay, but with huge numbers of nuclei the overall pattern is very predictable: the **half-life** is the time for half the undecayed nuclei to decay, or for the activity to halve. You must read half-lives from decay graphs and, at Higher tier, use half-life to calculate the **net decline** in activity as a ratio after a number of half-lives.

core.p: The **activity** of a radioactive source is the **rate at which the unstable nuclei in it decay**, in other words the number of nuclei that decay each second. It is measured in **becquerels (Bq)**.
bullets: **1 becquerel = 1 decay per second**.
Activity depends on how many undecayed nuclei there are and how unstable they are.
Large activities are given with prefixes: 1 kBq = 1000 Bq, 1 MBq = 1 000 000 Bq.
As a source decays there are fewer undecayed nuclei left, so the activity **decreases** with time.
Activity is a property of the source; it is not the same as the count rate a detector measures.

callouts.p: The rate at which the unstable nuclei of a source decay, measured in becquerels (Bq).
The unit of activity: one becquerel is one nuclear decay per second.

core.p: In the lab we measure radioactivity with a **Geiger-Muller (GM) tube** connected to a counter. The **count rate** is the number of counts detected per second (or per minute). It is always **less than the activity** because not every emission reaches the detector.
bullets: Radiation is emitted in **all directions**, and the GM tube only catches the part heading towards it.
Some radiation is absorbed by air or by the source itself before it reaches the tube.
The detector does not register every particle that enters it.
Count rate is still **proportional** to activity, so it halves when activity halves. This means you can find half-life from count rate data.
**Background radiation** must be measured separately and **subtracted** from each reading to get the corrected count rate of the source.

callouts.p: If a question gives a background count, subtract it from every reading BEFORE halving. Halving the uncorrected count gives the wrong half-life.

core.p: Radioactive decay is **random**. This means it is **impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when a particular nucleus will decay**. Each nucleus has a fixed chance of decaying in a given time, and that chance is not affected by external conditions.
bullets: You cannot say when an individual nucleus will decay.
Decay is **spontaneous**: it is not triggered by anything outside the nucleus.
Temperature, pressure and chemical combination do **not** change the rate of decay.
Evidence of randomness: repeated counts over equal time intervals give **different readings that fluctuate** around an average.
Because a source contains a **very large number of nuclei**, the random behaviour of individual nuclei averages out, so the **overall rate of decay is predictable**.
This is why half-life is a fixed value for each isotope even though decay is random.

callouts.p: Individual decays are random and unpredictable, but for a large number of nuclei the proportion that decays in a given time is constant, so half-life can be predicted.

core.p: The **half-life** of a radioactive isotope is the **time taken for half the undecayed nuclei to decay**, or equivalently the **time taken for the activity of a source to halve**. Every isotope has its own half-life, and it stays the same however much of the isotope you start with.
bullets: After 1 half-life, 1/2 of the original undecayed nuclei remain.
After 2 half-lives, 1/4 remain. After 3 half-lives, 1/8 remain. After 4 half-lives, 1/16 remain.
After n half-lives the fraction remaining is (1/2) to the power n.
The amount **never reaches zero** in a simple model; it keeps halving.
Half-lives range from fractions of a second to billions of years.
A **short half-life** means the nuclei are very unstable and the activity drops quickly.
A **long half-life** means the activity falls slowly and the source stays radioactive for a long time.

callouts.p: The time taken for half the undecayed nuclei in a sample to decay, or for the activity of a source to fall to half its original value.

core.h: Reading half-life from a decay graph
core.p: A graph of activity (or count rate, or number of undecayed nuclei) against time is a **curve that falls steeply at first and then levels off**. It falls quickly at first because there are many nuclei to decay, and more slowly later because there are fewer left. This shape is called **exponential decay**.
bullets: Step 1: read the starting activity on the y-axis, for example 800 Bq.
Step 2: halve it (400 Bq) and draw a horizontal line across to the curve.
Step 3: draw a vertical line down to the time axis and read the time. This is the half-life.
Step 4: check by halving again (400 to 200 Bq): the time interval should be the same.
You can start from **any** point on the curve; the time to halve is always the same.
Draw construction lines clearly on the graph: examiners often award a mark for them.

callouts.p: For accuracy, measure the time for several halvings (for example 800 to 100 Bq is 3 half-lives) and divide by the number of half-lives.

fig.cap: A decay curve for a source with a half-life of 2 hours. The activity halves from 800 Bq to 400 Bq in 2 hours, to 200 Bq after 4 hours and to 100 Bq after 6 hours. Dashed construction lines show how to read the half-life.

core.h: Why the decay curve has this shape
core.p: Because each nucleus has the same fixed chance of decaying per second, the **number that decay each second is proportional to the number still undecayed**. That one idea explains the whole shape of the graph.
bullets: At the start there are lots of undecayed nuclei, so lots decay per second: the graph is **steep**.
Later there are fewer undecayed nuclei, so fewer decay per second: the graph is **shallower**.
The activity itself therefore falls, which is why activity and number of undecayed nuclei have the **same-shaped** curve and the **same half-life**.
The curve gets closer and closer to zero but, in theory, never reaches it.
Real data points scatter around a smooth curve because decay is random; draw a **smooth best-fit curve**, not dot-to-dot lines.

core.p: A common class model of random decay uses a large number of dice (or coins). Each die represents a nucleus. Throw them all; every die that lands on a six has 'decayed' and is removed. Count the remaining dice and repeat.
bullets: You cannot predict which die will show a six: like a single nucleus, each one is random.
Each die has the same chance (1/6) of 'decaying' on each throw, like each nucleus has a fixed probability.
With many dice, the number remaining after each throw falls in a smooth, predictable way.
Plotting dice remaining against number of throws gives a **decay curve** with a constant 'half-life' of about 4 throws.
Using more dice gives a smoother curve, showing why large numbers of nuclei give predictable results.
The throw number represents time; the dice removed per throw represent activity.

fig.cap: Dice model of radioactive decay. Each throw removes dice showing a six. With 600 dice, about 1/6 decay each throw, and the number left roughly halves every 4 throws: random for one die, predictable for many.

core.p: Many questions ask how much of a sample, or what activity, is left after a certain time, or ask you to find the half-life from data. Always work in **whole numbers of half-lives** by repeatedly halving.
bullets: Find the number of half-lives: n = time elapsed / half-life.
Halve the starting value n times (or multiply by (1/2) to the power n).
To find the time: count how many halvings take the value from start to finish, then multiply by the half-life.
To find the half-life from a table: find two readings where one is half the other and subtract the times.
Mass of a radioactive isotope remaining halves in the same way as activity, because activity is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei.
Always quote units: hours, days, years, Bq, counts per minute.

callouts.p: Write 800 -> 400 -> 200 -> 100 with the time under each arrow. It is quick, clear and examiners can award method marks.

core.h: Net decline as a ratio (Higher tier)
core.p: At Higher tier you must use the half-life to calculate the **net decline**, expressed as a **ratio**, in the activity of a source after a given number of half-lives. The ratio compares the final activity with the initial activity.
bullets: After n half-lives, final activity : initial activity = 1 : 2 to the power n.
After 3 half-lives: activity falls to 1/8 of its starting value, so the ratio of final to initial is **1 : 8**.
The **net decline** is the amount lost: after 3 half-lives the activity has fallen by 7/8 of its original value.
Example: initial activity 480 Bq, 4 half-lives pass. Final = 480 / 16 = 30 Bq. Ratio final : initial = 30 : 480 = 1 : 16. Net decline = 480 - 30 = 450 Bq, which is 15/16 of the original.
Read the question carefully: 'ratio of final to initial', 'fraction remaining' and 'fraction decayed' are different answers.
Simplify ratios fully, for example 25 : 400 = 1 : 16.

callouts.p: After 2 half-lives 1/4 REMAINS, so 3/4 has DECAYED. Many students give 1/4 when asked how much has decayed.

fig.cap: Bar chart of activity after each half-life for a source starting at 480 Bq. After 4 half-lives the activity is 30 Bq, so the ratio of final to initial activity is 1 : 16 and the net decline is 450 Bq.
