core.p: In an experiment a GM tube is held a fixed distance from a source with a short half-life (for example protactinium-234) and the count rate is recorded at regular intervals. The half-life is found from a graph of corrected count rate against time.
bullets: Measure the **background count rate** first with no source present.
Keep the distance between source and GM tube **fixed**, since moving it changes the count rate.
Record count rate at regular time intervals.
Subtract background from every reading to get the **corrected count rate**.
Plot corrected count rate against time and draw a smooth curve of best fit.
Read the time for the count rate to halve from several starting points and take a **mean** for a more reliable half-life.
Readings fluctuate because decay is random; longer counting times reduce the effect of this.

core.p: Half-life lets scientists predict how long a source stays active and how its activity changes, even though individual decays are random. Grade 9 answers connect the random behaviour of nuclei to the predictable behaviour of a sample.
bullets: Large numbers of nuclei make the overall decay rate statistically predictable.
Half-life is constant for an isotope because each nucleus has a fixed probability of decaying.
Doubling the amount of an isotope doubles its activity but does **not** change its half-life.
Comparing two isotopes: the one with the shorter half-life has a higher activity for the same number of nuclei but becomes safe more quickly.
Half-life cannot be changed by heating, cooling or chemical reactions.

callouts.t: Half-life does not depend on amount
callouts.p: A 1 g sample and a 100 g sample of the same isotope have the same half-life; the larger sample just has a larger activity.

analogy.p: Imagine a pan full of popcorn kernels being heated. You cannot predict which kernel will pop next or when (random), but with thousands of kernels you can predict that roughly the same fraction of the remaining kernels pops every few seconds. At first there are lots of pops per second (high activity); as fewer unpopped kernels remain, the popping slows (activity falls). The time for half the unpopped kernels to pop is like the half-life. Where it breaks down: popcorn pops because it is heated, but radioactive decay is not affected by temperature at all; and a real popcorn pan runs out of kernels, whereas a radioactive sample with huge numbers of nuclei keeps halving smoothly.

terms.d: The rate at which the unstable nuclei of a source decay.
The unit of activity; 1 Bq = 1 decay per second.
The number of decays detected per second or per minute by a detector such as a GM tube.
A detector that produces a pulse (a count) each time ionising radiation enters it.
Low-level ionising radiation that is always present; it must be subtracted from measured count rates.
Measured count rate minus the background count rate.
It is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay or when a particular nucleus will decay.
Decay happens without any outside cause and is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical conditions.
The time taken for half the undecayed nuclei to decay, or for the activity of a source to halve.
Unstable nuclei in a sample that have not yet decayed.
A graph of activity or undecayed nuclei against time that falls steeply then levels off, halving in equal time intervals.
A decrease in which the quantity falls by the same fraction in each equal time interval.
The overall decrease in activity after a number of half-lives, often expressed as a ratio of final to initial activity.

terms.t: Ratio of final to initial activity
terms.d: After n half-lives this is 1 : 2 to the power n, for example 1 : 8 after 3 half-lives.
Each nucleus of a given isotope has the same fixed chance of decaying in a given time.

mistakes.w: Half-life is half the time it takes for a source to completely decay.
mistakes.r: Half-life is the time for half the undecayed nuclei to decay, or for the activity to halve. A source never completely decays in this model.

mistakes.w: Half-life is the time for half the mass of the source to disappear.
mistakes.r: Say half the undecayed (radioactive) nuclei decay; the daughter nuclei are still there, so the sample's mass hardly changes.

mistakes.w: After two half-lives the source has completely decayed.
mistakes.r: After two half-lives 1/4 of the undecayed nuclei remain.

mistakes.w: Random decay means we cannot predict anything about the source.
mistakes.r: We cannot predict when an individual nucleus decays, but with large numbers the half-life and overall rate are predictable.

mistakes.w: Heating a source makes it decay faster.
mistakes.r: Decay rate and half-life are not affected by temperature or other physical or chemical conditions.

mistakes.w: Halving the raw count rate without subtracting background.
mistakes.r: Subtract the background count rate from every reading first, then find when the corrected count rate halves.

mistakes.w: Activity is measured in counts per minute.
mistakes.r: Activity is measured in becquerels (decays per second); counts per minute is a count rate measured by a detector.

mistakes.w: After 3 half-lives the ratio of final to initial activity is 1 : 6.
mistakes.r: Activity halves each time: 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/8, so the ratio is 1 : 8.

mistakes.w: A bigger sample has a longer half-life.
mistakes.r: Half-life is the same for any amount of the same isotope; a bigger sample has a bigger activity.

exam.q: State what is meant by the activity of a radioactive source.
model: The rate at which unstable nuclei decay / number of decays per second
exam.tip: Use the word 'rate' or 'per second'.

exam.q: State the unit of activity.
model: Becquerel (Bq)
exam.tip: Spell it correctly or use Bq.

exam.q: Define the half-life of a radioactive isotope.
model: Time taken for half the (undecayed) nuclei to decay
or time for the activity (count rate) to halve
exam.tip: Always include 'time taken' and 'half'.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by radioactive decay being random.
model: Cannot predict which nucleus will decay next
Cannot predict when a particular nucleus will decay
exam.tip: Refer to individual nuclei.

exam.q: A student records count rates from a source over equal time intervals. The readings are not exactly the same. Suggest why.
model: Radioactive decay is random
exam.tip: Fluctuations in repeated readings are evidence of randomness.

exam.q: A source has an activity of 640 Bq and a half-life of 3 days. Calculate its activity after 12 days.
model: Number of half-lives = 12 / 3 = 4
Activity = 40 Bq
exam.tip: Show the halving chain for method marks.

exam.q: The count rate from a source falls from 1200 counts per minute to 150 counts per minute in 45 minutes. Calculate the half-life.
model: Half-life = 45 / 3
= 15 minutes
exam.tip: Count halvings first, then divide the total time.

exam.q: (Higher) A source has a half-life of 8 hours. Calculate the ratio of its final activity to its initial activity after 32 hours.
model: 32 / 8 = 4 half-lives
Ratio = 1 : 16
exam.tip: Ratio after n half-lives is 1 : 2 to the power n.

exam.q: (Higher) The initial activity of a sample is 3200 Bq. After 5 half-lives, calculate the net decline in activity.
model: Final activity = 3200 / 32 = 100 Bq
Net decline = 3200 - 100
= 3100 Bq (ratio of final to initial 1 : 32)
exam.tip: Net decline is how much the activity has fallen, not how much remains.

exam.q: Explain why the half-life of a radioactive isotope can be predicted even though radioactive decay is random.
model: Each nucleus has the same fixed probability of decaying in a given time
A sample contains a very large number of nuclei
So the random behaviour of individual nuclei averages out
A constant proportion decays in each time interval, so the time to halve is constant
exam.tip: Link individual randomness to large-number statistics.

exam.q: Describe how a student could use a GM tube and counter to determine the half-life of a radioactive source. Include how the data should be processed.
model: Measure background count rate with no source present
Place source at a fixed distance from the GM tube
Record the count rate at regular time intervals
Subtract background from each reading to get corrected count rate
Plot corrected count rate against time and draw a smooth curve
Read the time for the count rate to halve from several points and take a mean
exam.tip: Six-markers need a logical sequence: background, measure, correct, plot, read, average.

worked.q: Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days. A sample has an activity of 2400 Bq. Find its activity after 24 days and the fraction of the original nuclei that has decayed.
steps: Number of half-lives = 24 / 8 = 3.
Fraction remaining = (1/2) to the power 3 = 1/8.
Fraction decayed = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8.
worked.ans: Activity = 300 Bq; 7/8 of the original nuclei have decayed.

worked.q: A GM tube records 520 counts per minute from a source. The background count is 20 counts per minute. Forty minutes later the reading is 145 counts per minute. Find the half-life.
steps: Corrected initial count = 520 - 20 = 500 counts per minute.
Corrected final count = 145 - 20 = 125 counts per minute.
500 -> 250 -> 125 is 2 half-lives.
Half-life = 40 / 2 = 20 minutes.
worked.ans: Half-life = 20 minutes.

worked.q: (Higher) A medical source has an initial activity of 96 MBq and a half-life of 6 hours. Calculate the ratio of final to initial activity and the net decline after 30 hours.
steps: Number of half-lives = 30 / 6 = 5.
Final activity = 96 / 2 to the power 5 = 96 / 32 = 3 MBq.
Ratio final : initial = 3 : 96 = 1 : 32.
Net decline = 96 - 3 = 93 MBq.
worked.ans: Ratio 1 : 32; net decline 93 MBq (activity has fallen by 31/32).

phy_edx.5.8.summary: Radioactive sources are useful because their radiation can **ionise**, **penetrate** materials by different amounts and **kill cells**, and because it can be **detected** from outside. The Edexcel spec names five uses: **household smoke alarms**, **irradiating food**, **sterilising equipment**, **tracing and gauging thicknesses**, and **diagnosis and treatment of cancer**. For each use you must be able to explain which radiation (alpha, beta or gamma) is chosen and why, using its penetrating power, ionising power and the half-life of the source.

core.p: Every use of radioactivity depends on matching the properties of the radiation and the isotope to the job. Grade 9 answers always justify the choice using **penetration**, **ionisation** and **half-life**.
bullets: **Alpha**: very strongly ionising, stopped by paper or a few cm of air. Useful only where the radiation must not escape and must ionise strongly (smoke alarms).
**Beta**: moderately ionising, passes through paper but is stopped by a few mm of aluminium. Useful for gauging thin sheets.
**Gamma**: weakly ionising, very penetrating, only reduced by thick lead or concrete. Useful when radiation must pass through packaging, metal or the body.
**Half-life** must suit the job: long enough to last the time needed, but not so long that the source stays dangerous unnecessarily.
A source that must be detected outside an object (tracers, gauges) must emit radiation that can **penetrate** that object.
A source used inside the body should be **weakly ionising** (usually gamma) and have a **short half-life** to limit damage.

head: Radiation
Ionising power
Stopped by
Typical use
rows: Paper, skin, few cm of air
Thickness gauging of paper, thin metal

callouts.p: Must the radiation get out or through something? How strongly must it ionise? How long must the source last?

core.p: Smoke alarms contain a small **alpha source**, usually **americium-241**. The alpha particles **ionise the air** between two charged plates, so the air conducts and a **small current** flows. When smoke enters, the smoke particles **absorb the alpha particles**, so less air is ionised, the **current falls**, and the circuit detects this drop and **sounds the alarm**.
bullets: Alpha is used because it is **strongly ionising**, so it produces plenty of ions in the air gap.
Alpha has **low penetration**: it is stopped by the casing and a few cm of air, so it does not escape into the room.
Smoke absorbs alpha easily, which is what makes the detector sensitive.
Americium-241 has a **long half-life (about 430 years)**, so the activity stays almost constant over the life of the alarm and the source never needs replacing.
Beta or gamma would not work well: they are too weakly ionising and would pass through smoke with little absorption.

callouts.p: Alpha ionises air -> current flows -> smoke absorbs alpha -> fewer ions -> current drops -> alarm sounds. Missing a link loses a mark.

fig.cap: Smoke alarm. Alpha particles from americium-241 ionise the air between two charged plates so a small current flows. Smoke absorbs the alpha particles, the current falls and the alarm sounds.

core.p: Food can be exposed to a strong source of **gamma radiation** to **kill bacteria, mould and insects**. This makes the food safer to eat and helps it **stay fresh for longer** (longer shelf life).
bullets: Gamma is used because it is **highly penetrating**: it passes through packaging and into the whole of the food, so the food can be treated after it is sealed.
The gamma radiation damages the DNA of microbes, killing them or stopping them reproducing.
Food that is **irradiated does not become radioactive**: it is exposed to radiation but does not contain the source. This is irradiation, not contamination.
A common source is cobalt-60, which emits gamma rays and has a half-life of about 5 years, so it lasts a long time before replacement.
The treatment can be done at room temperature without cooking the food.
Some people worry it may change taste or nutrients slightly, and it does not remove toxins that bacteria have already made.

callouts.p: A very common wrong answer is that irradiated food becomes radioactive. It does not, because no radioactive material is left in or on the food.

core.p: Medical equipment such as syringes, scalpels, dressings and surgical gloves is sterilised by exposing it to **gamma radiation**, which **kills bacteria and other microorganisms**.
bullets: Gamma passes through the **sealed packaging**, so the equipment is sterilised after packing and stays sterile until it is opened.
It works on **heat-sensitive items** such as plastic syringes that would melt if boiled or heated in an autoclave.
The items are irradiated, not contaminated, so they are **not made radioactive** and are safe to use.
Alpha and beta could not be used because they would be stopped by the packaging and would not reach all surfaces.
The source is shielded in thick concrete or lead and the items pass by it on a conveyor.

core.p: A **tracer** is a small amount of radioactive isotope added to a liquid or gas so that its movement can be **followed from outside** with a detector. For example, a tracer added to water in an underground pipe shows where the pipe is leaking: the detector on the surface picks up a **higher count rate** above the leak, where the tracer collects in the soil.
bullets: The tracer must emit **gamma** (or sometimes high-energy beta) so the radiation can **penetrate** the pipe and soil to reach the detector.
Alpha would be useless because it would be absorbed before reaching the surface.
The isotope should have a **short half-life**, typically a few hours to days: long enough to complete the test, short enough that it does not stay in the environment.
Tracers can also show where fluids flow in pipes, how fertiliser is taken up by plants, and how pollutants spread.
The daughter product should be **stable** or harmless.

fig.cap: Leak detection with a gamma tracer. Water containing the tracer leaks out of an underground pipe and collects in the soil. A detector moved along the surface records a much higher count rate above the leak.

core.p: Radioactive sources are used to **monitor and control the thickness** of materials such as paper, plastic film and aluminium foil as they are made. A source is placed on one side of the sheet and a detector on the other. If the sheet becomes **thicker**, more radiation is absorbed and the **count rate falls**; if it becomes **thinner**, the count rate **rises**. The signal is fed back to the rollers to adjust the pressure and keep the thickness constant.
bullets: For paper, plastic and thin aluminium a **beta** source is used: beta is **partly absorbed**, so small changes in thickness cause a **measurable change** in count rate.
Alpha would be **completely stopped** by the sheet, so the count rate would be zero whatever the thickness.
Gamma would **pass straight through** thin sheets almost unaffected, so changes in thickness would barely change the count rate.
For **thick steel sheets**, gamma is used because beta would be completely absorbed.
The source needs a **long half-life** so its activity stays roughly constant; otherwise a falling count rate could be mistaken for the sheet getting thicker.
The rule is: choose the radiation that is partly absorbed by the thickness being measured.

callouts.p: Top answers say why beta is used AND why alpha (all absorbed) and gamma (hardly any absorbed) would not work.

fig.cap: Thickness gauge for paper. A beta source sits under the sheet and a detector above it. If the count rate drops, the paper is too thick and the control unit increases the roller pressure; if it rises, the pressure is reduced.

core.p: Radioactive isotopes are used to **find (diagnose)** cancers and other problems inside the body. A **medical tracer** is injected or swallowed; it travels to the organ or tumour being investigated, and the radiation it emits is detected outside the body to build up an image. Details of tracers and PET scanning belong to a separate spec point, but you need the reasons here.
bullets: The tracer must emit **gamma** (or positrons that produce gamma rays, as in PET) so the radiation can **pass out of the body** to the detector.
Gamma is **weakly ionising**, so it causes less damage to cells as it passes through.
It must have a **short half-life** (hours), so the patient's exposure is low and the activity soon falls, but long enough to complete the scan.
Example: technetium-99m, a gamma emitter with a half-life of about 6 hours.
Tumours may absorb more of the tracer, showing up as 'hot spots' with higher count rate.

core.p: Ionising radiation **kills cells** or damages their DNA so they cannot divide. This is harmful to healthy tissue, but it can be used deliberately to **destroy cancer cells**. This is called **radiotherapy**.
bullets: **External beam**: carefully aimed beams of gamma rays are directed at the tumour from **different angles**, so the tumour gets a high dose while surrounding healthy tissue gets a smaller dose.

**Internal**: a radioactive source, often a beta emitter, is placed inside or next to the tumour, or a radioactive substance that collects in the tumour is given (for example iodine-131 for thyroid cancer).
Beta sources placed internally act over a **short range**, so the damage is concentrated in the tumour.
The dose is planned so that the benefit of killing cancer cells **outweighs the risk** of damaging healthy cells.
Side effects such as tiredness and sickness happen because some healthy cells are also damaged.

callouts.p: Diagnosis needs radiation that passes OUT of the body and does little damage. Treatment needs radiation that DOES damage cells, but only in the tumour.

core.h: Why half-life matters for each use
core.p: Choosing the half-life is a balance between the source lasting long enough to do its job and not remaining dangerous for longer than necessary.
bullets: Smoke alarm: **long** half-life (about 430 years) so it works for the alarm's whole life.
Thickness gauge: **long** half-life so the count rate changes only because of the thickness, not because the source is decaying.
Sterilising and food irradiation: fairly **long** half-life (cobalt-60, about 5 years) so the source does not need frequent replacement.
Industrial tracers: **short** half-life so the tracer does not stay radioactive in the soil or water.
Medical tracers: **short** half-life (hours) to reduce the dose to the patient.
Internal radiotherapy: a half-life of days, so the source delivers its dose and then decays.

head: Use
Radiation
Half-life needed
Key reason
rows: Strongly ionises air; does not escape
Detected through soil; does not linger
Partly absorbed, so changes are measurable

core.p: All these uses involve ionising radiation, so the benefits must be weighed against risks. Workers and the public are protected by shielding and by keeping exposure as low as possible.
bullets: Sources are kept in **shielded containers** (lead or thick concrete) when not in use.
Workers handle sources with **tongs**, stay as far away as possible and limit their time near the source.
Workers may wear **dosimeters** to monitor their exposure.
The tiny alpha source in a smoke alarm is safe in normal use because alpha cannot get through the casing, but it must not be taken apart or swallowed.
Using a source with a suitable half-life reduces the time it remains hazardous after use.

core.h: How to answer 'explain the choice of source' questions
core.p: Edexcel often describes an unfamiliar application and gives a table of isotopes with their radiation type and half-life, asking you to choose the best one. Use a structured approach.
bullets: Step 1: decide whether the radiation must **pass through** something (skin, packaging, soil, metal) or must be **absorbed**.
Step 2: rule out radiations that are too weakly or too strongly absorbed.
Step 3: decide whether the half-life should be **long** (source must last) or **short** (must not linger in a body or environment).
Step 4: pick the isotope that fits both and **give a reason for each** choice.
Step 5: if relevant, mention that the daughter product should be stable or not harmful.
Avoid vague answers like 'it is safer'; say exactly why, for example 'gamma is weakly ionising so less damage to cells'.

callouts.p: Most 'choose a source' questions give one mark for the radiation type reason and one for the half-life reason.

analogy.t: Choosing the right tool from a toolbox
analogy.p: Alpha, beta and gamma are like three tools. Alpha is a hammer: powerful but with a very short reach, ideal for a sealed box like a smoke alarm where it must hit hard close by and never escape. Beta is a pair of scissors: it cuts through thin material like paper but jams on thick metal, so how much gets through tells you the thickness. Gamma is an X-ray torch: it shines right through packaging, soil and the body, perfect for sterilising sealed packs or tracing a leak from outside. Half-life is like the battery life of the tool: some jobs need a battery that lasts years, others need one that runs out within hours so the tool switches itself off. Where it breaks down: tools are only dangerous if misused, but every radioactive source causes some ionisation and risk, so the benefit must always be weighed against the harm.

terms.d: Radiation that can knock electrons out of atoms, turning them into ions.
How far radiation can travel through a material before being absorbed.
An isotope that emits alpha particles; strongly ionising and stopped by paper or a few cm of air.
An isotope that emits beta particles; moderately ionising and stopped by a few mm of aluminium.
An isotope that emits gamma rays; weakly ionising and very penetrating.
An alpha-emitting isotope with a long half-life, used in household smoke alarms.
A device in which alpha particles ionise air to give a current; smoke absorbs the alpha, the current falls and the alarm sounds.
Exposing an object to radiation from outside; the object does not become radioactive.
Radioactive material getting onto or into an object or person, which then continues to be exposed.
Using gamma rays to kill bacteria and insects in food so it lasts longer.
Killing all microorganisms on an object; gamma rays can sterilise sealed medical equipment.
A radioactive isotope added to a substance so its movement can be followed with a detector.
A system using a source and detector on either side of a sheet to monitor and control its thickness.
The time taken for the activity of a source to halve; it decides how long a source stays useful and hazardous.
Using ionising radiation to kill cancer cells.
A short half-life gamma-emitting isotope put into the body to produce images for diagnosis.

mistakes.w: Irradiated food is radioactive and unsafe to eat.
mistakes.r: Irradiated food is not radioactive because it was only exposed to gamma radiation and contains no radioactive source.

mistakes.w: Smoke alarms work because smoke stops gamma rays.
mistakes.r: Smoke alarms use alpha particles, which ionise air to produce a current; smoke absorbs the alpha particles so the current falls.

mistakes.w: Smoke alarms use alpha because it is the safest radiation.
mistakes.r: Alpha is used because it is strongly ionising (ionises the air) and has a short range, so it does not escape the alarm.

mistakes.w: Gamma is used to gauge the thickness of paper.
mistakes.r: Beta is used for paper because it is partly absorbed; gamma would pass through almost unchanged.

mistakes.w: Alpha is used for thickness gauging because it is absorbed by paper.
mistakes.r: Alpha would be completely absorbed whatever the thickness, so the count rate would not change.

mistakes.w: Tracers should have a long half-life so they last.
mistakes.r: Tracers need a short half-life so they do not remain radioactive in the body or environment, but long enough to complete the test.

mistakes.w: Medical tracers use alpha because it is easy to detect.
mistakes.r: Medical tracers use gamma because it can pass out of the body to the detector and is weakly ionising.

mistakes.w: Sterilising with gamma makes the equipment radioactive.
mistakes.r: The equipment is irradiated, not contaminated, so it does not become radioactive.

mistakes.w: The gauge source can have a short half-life.
mistakes.r: A gauge needs a long half-life so the count rate only changes because of thickness, not source decay.

exam.q: Name the type of radiation used in a household smoke alarm.
model: Alpha
exam.tip: One word is enough for a 1-mark state question.

exam.q: Explain why the source in a smoke alarm needs a long half-life.
model: So the activity stays (almost) constant
so the alarm works for many years without replacing the source
exam.tip: Link half-life to how long the device is used.

exam.q: Explain how a smoke alarm detects smoke.
model: Alpha particles ionise the air between the plates
So a (small) current flows
Smoke absorbs the alpha particles / less ionisation
Current falls and this triggers the alarm
exam.tip: Give the complete chain in order.

exam.q: Explain why gamma radiation is used to sterilise medical equipment.
model: Gamma kills bacteria / microorganisms
Gamma is very penetrating so it passes through the packaging
exam.tip: Mention the sealed packaging.

exam.q: A student says that food which has been irradiated becomes radioactive. Explain why the student is wrong.
model: The food is only exposed to radiation (irradiated)
No radioactive material is left in or on the food (not contaminated)
exam.tip: Use the words irradiation and contamination correctly.

exam.q: Give one advantage of irradiating food.
model: Kills bacteria so food lasts longer / safer to eat
exam.tip: Be specific about bacteria or shelf life.

exam.q: A radioactive tracer is used to find a leak in an underground water pipe. State and explain the type of radiation and the half-life the tracer should have.
model: Gamma
Can penetrate the soil to reach the detector at the surface
Short half-life
So it does not remain radioactive in the ground / water supply for long
exam.tip: Two marks for radiation type and reason, two for half-life and reason.

exam.q: Explain why a beta source, rather than an alpha or gamma source, is used to monitor the thickness of paper in a factory.
model: Beta is partly absorbed by paper so changes in thickness change the count rate
Alpha would be completely absorbed by the paper
Gamma would pass through with almost no change in count rate
exam.tip: Address all three radiations.

exam.q: State two ways that radioactivity is used in the diagnosis and treatment of cancer.
model: Tracer (gamma emitter) injected to locate a tumour / produce an image
Gamma rays (or implanted sources) used to kill cancer cells (radiotherapy)
exam.tip: One diagnosis use and one treatment use.

exam.q: Describe how a radioactive source can be used in a factory to keep the thickness of aluminium foil constant. Explain your choice of source.
model: Source on one side of the foil and detector on the other
Count rate measured continuously
If the foil gets thicker the count rate falls; thinner, it rises
Signal sent to rollers to change pressure and correct thickness
Use a beta source because it is partly absorbed by thin aluminium so changes are measurable
Long half-life so the count rate only changes because of thickness
exam.tip: Cover the set-up, the feedback, the choice of radiation and the half-life.

worked.q: A company needs a source for a thickness gauge for paper. Choose from: Source A alpha, half-life 400 years; Source B beta, half-life 30 years; Source C gamma, half-life 5 years; Source D beta, half-life 2 hours. Explain your choice.
steps: Paper must partly absorb the radiation so the count rate depends on thickness: this rules out alpha (fully absorbed) and gamma (barely absorbed).
That leaves the beta sources B and D.
The source must have a long half-life so its activity stays steady during production; D would decay noticeably within hours.
Source B is beta with a 30 year half-life, so it fits both requirements.
worked.ans: Source B: beta is partly absorbed by paper, and its long half-life means changes in count rate are due to thickness, not decay.

worked.q: A hospital wants a tracer to image a patient's kidneys. Choose from: P alpha, half-life 6 hours; Q gamma, half-life 6 hours; R gamma, half-life 30 years. Explain your choice.
steps: The radiation must leave the body to reach the camera, so alpha (P) is ruled out; it would be absorbed inside the patient and is strongly ionising.
Gamma is penetrating and weakly ionising, so Q or R.
The half-life should be short to reduce the patient's dose but long enough to do the scan: 6 hours fits; 30 years would keep the patient radioactive for far too long.
Choose Q.
worked.ans: Source Q: gamma passes out of the body and is weakly ionising, and a 6 hour half-life is long enough for the scan but short enough to limit the dose.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why cobalt-60 (gamma emitter, half-life about 5 years) is suitable for sterilising packaged syringes.
steps: Gamma rays kill bacteria and other microorganisms.
Gamma is highly penetrating so it passes through the sealed packaging and reaches every surface of the syringe.
The syringes are irradiated, not contaminated, so they are not made radioactive.
No heating is needed, so plastic syringes do not melt.
A half-life of about 5 years means the source lasts a long time before it needs replacing.
worked.ans: Cobalt-60 emits penetrating gamma rays that kill microbes through sealed packaging without heating or making the syringes radioactive, and its long half-life gives a long working life.

phy_edx.5.9.summary: Ionising radiation knocks electrons off atoms in living cells, which can **kill cells** or **damage DNA**, causing **mutations** that may lead to **cancer**. Because of this, anyone working with radioactive sources follows **precautions** that reduce the dose: shielding, distance, short exposure time and monitoring. You must also be able to tell **irradiation** (being exposed to radiation from a source outside you) apart from **contamination** (radioactive atoms getting on or into you), compare their hazards for alpha, beta and gamma, and explain the problems of **disposing of radioactive waste**.

core.p: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation (and neutrons) are **ionising**: as they pass through matter they knock electrons out of atoms, turning them into **ions**. In the body this happens to the atoms and molecules that make up cells, including **DNA**. Ionising a molecule can break bonds or create reactive chemicals, so the molecule stops working properly.
bullets: Ionisation inside a cell can **damage or kill the cell**.
Ionisation of DNA can cause a **mutation** (a change in the genetic code).
A mutated cell may **divide uncontrollably**, which is **cancer**.
Mutations in sex cells (sperm or eggs) can be **passed on to offspring**.
Large doses cause radiation sickness and burns because many cells are killed at once.
The more ionising the radiation that reaches the cells, the greater the damage.

callouts.p: radiation reaches cells -> ionises atoms/molecules -> damages DNA -> mutation -> uncontrolled cell division -> cancer. Exam answers that skip the word **ionises** often lose the first mark.

fig.cap: Ionising radiation passing through a cell ionises molecules in the nucleus and can damage DNA. A large dose kills the cell; a smaller dose may cause a mutation, and the mutated cell may divide uncontrollably, forming a tumour (cancer).

core.p: The spec asks you to describe how ionising radiation **can cause mutations in living organisms** and **can damage cells and tissue**. These are two different outcomes and examiners like both.
bullets: **Mutation**: DNA is changed but the cell survives; the risk is cancer later, possibly many years after exposure.
**Cell death**: the cell is destroyed; lots of dead cells means **tissue damage**, burns or organ failure.
Rapidly dividing cells (bone marrow, gut lining, skin, reproductive organs, a developing foetus) are most easily harmed.
The risk of harm increases with the **dose** received: a bigger dose means more ionisation and more chance of damage.
Even a small dose carries a small risk, so doses should be kept **as low as reasonably practicable**.

core.h: Ionising power and penetration decide the danger
core.p: How dangerous a radiation is depends on two properties you met earlier: how strongly it **ionises** and how far it **penetrates**. These pull in opposite directions, which is why the location of the source matters so much.

head: Radiation
Ionising power
Penetration
Stopped by
rows: Paper or the outer layer of dead skin
Reduced by thick lead or concrete

bullets: Alpha is **most ionising** so does the most damage to any cells it reaches, but it cannot get through skin.
Gamma passes through the body easily, so it ionises only a little along its path but can reach organs from outside.
Beta is in between on both counts.

core.p: **Irradiation** is when a person or object is exposed to radiation from a source **outside** it. The radiation travels from the source to the person. Once the source is removed or shielded, the exposure **stops**.
bullets: An irradiated object **does not become radioactive** (gamma-irradiated food is safe to eat).
Hazard depends on how penetrating the radiation is: gamma and beta from outside can reach living cells; alpha from outside cannot get through the dead outer layer of skin.
Examples: having an X-ray, working near a sealed gamma source, sterilising medical equipment with gamma rays.
Reduce irradiation by **shielding, distance and time**.

callouts.p: Exposure of an object or person to ionising radiation from a source outside it. The object does not become radioactive.

core.p: **Contamination** is when radioactive **atoms (material)** get **onto or into** a person or object, for example by touching, breathing in dust or gas, eating or drinking. The radioactive atoms are now carried with you and **keep decaying**, so the exposure continues until they are removed or have decayed.
bullets: Contamination is **hard to remove**, especially once material has been breathed in or swallowed.
The source is now **in direct contact with cells**, so even alpha can reach living tissue.
Contaminated objects are radioactive and can **spread contamination** to others.
Example: breathing in radon gas, which decays in the lungs; touching a radioactive source with bare hands.
Reduce contamination with **gloves, tongs, protective clothing, masks** and never eating or drinking near sources.

callouts.p: The unwanted presence of radioactive atoms (materials) on or inside an object or person.

callouts.t: Do not say irradiated things become radioactive
callouts.p: Only contamination leaves radioactive material behind. Irradiated food, or a patient after an X-ray, is not radioactive.

fig.cap: Irradiation (left): the source stays outside the body and the exposure ends when the source is removed; the person does not become radioactive. Contamination (right): radioactive atoms are on or in the body, keep decaying and are hard to remove.

core.h: Comparing the hazards of irradiation and contamination
core.p: Exam questions often ask which type of radiation is most dangerous **outside** the body and which is most dangerous **inside** the body. The answer flips for alpha, and you must explain why using ionisation and penetration.

head: Radiation
Source outside body (irradiation)
Source inside body (contamination)
rows: Low hazard: absorbed by skin or air, cannot reach living cells
Most dangerous: all energy deposited in nearby cells, strongly ionising
Hazardous: can penetrate skin and reach tissue
Hazardous: moderately ionising in surrounding tissue
Most dangerous outside: penetrates to internal organs
Less dangerous than alpha: most passes straight out of the body, weakly ionising

bullets: **Outside**: gamma and beta are the main danger because they penetrate.
**Inside**: alpha is the main danger because it is strongly ionising and cannot escape, so all its energy is absorbed in a small volume of tissue.
Contamination is generally **more hazardous** than irradiation because exposure continues for as long as the material stays in the body.

fig.cap: A qualitative comparison: alpha is the least hazardous source outside the body but the most hazardous inside it. Gamma is most hazardous from outside because it penetrates to organs, but much of it passes out of the body if swallowed.

core.p: All precautions work by reducing the **amount of radiation absorbed** by the body, or by stopping radioactive material getting onto or into it. The key ideas are **time, distance, shielding** and **preventing contamination**.
bullets: **Minimise time** of exposure: less time means fewer decays reach you.
**Maximise distance**: hold sources with **long-handled tongs** and keep them at arm's length; radiation spreads out and alpha and beta are absorbed by air.
**Shielding**: store sources in **lead-lined boxes**; use lead aprons and lead or concrete walls; radiographers stand behind screens.
**Never point a source at anyone** and label sources with the hazard symbol.
**Wear gloves and protective clothing** to stop contamination of skin; wash hands afterwards.
**Monitor dose** with a **dosimeter (film badge)** worn by workers, so that doses can be checked and kept below safe limits.
Use the **least active** source that will do the job and return it to storage straight after use.

callouts.p: For 2 marks give the precaution AND how it reduces risk, e.g. 'use tongs (1) so the source is further from the hand, so less radiation is absorbed (1)'.

fig.cap: School laboratory precautions: the source is kept in a lead-lined box, handled with long tongs at a distance, out for the minimum time and never pointed at anyone. Workers who use radiation regularly wear a dosimeter badge to monitor their dose.

core.h: Precautions for people who work with radiation
core.p: Hospital and nuclear industry workers are exposed every day, so their precautions are stricter and their doses are **monitored and limited**.
bullets: Radiographers leave the room or stand behind a **lead screen** when an X-ray or scan is taken.
Workers wear **dosimeter badges**; if a badge shows a high dose the worker is moved to other duties.
**Remote handling** (robot arms, manipulators behind thick lead-glass windows) keeps distance large for very active sources.
Protective suits and breathing masks prevent contamination where dust or gas may be present.
The patient's dose is also kept as low as possible: only the necessary part of the body is exposed, and the scan is only done when the benefit outweighs the risk.

core.h: Radioactive waste: what the problems are
core.p: The spec asks you to describe **problems arising in the disposal of radioactive waste** and how the risks can be reduced. Waste comes from nuclear power stations, hospitals and research. The main problem is that some waste stays radioactive for a **very long time**.
bullets: Some waste contains isotopes with **very long half-lives**, so it remains dangerous for **thousands of years**.
It must be stored so it **cannot leak** into groundwater, soil, the sea or the air, where it could contaminate food and drinking water.
Containers must last for a very long time without corroding, and the site must be geologically stable (no earthquakes, no water flow).
High-level waste is also **hot**, because decay releases energy, so it needs cooling.
Waste must be guarded so it cannot be stolen or misused, and future generations need to know it is there.
People often object to waste being stored or transported near where they live.

core.p: Risks are reduced by **containing** the waste, keeping it **away from people**, and **monitoring** it. The method depends on how radioactive the waste is.
bullets: **Low-level waste** (gloves, paper towels, protective clothing): sealed and buried in landfill-type sites.
**Higher-level waste**: sealed in steel containers, often after being set in **glass or concrete**, then stored **deep underground** in stable rock.
Storage sites are monitored for leaks.
Highly active spent fuel is first stored in **cooling ponds** of water, which also absorbs radiation.
Sites are chosen away from towns and from flowing water.

callouts.p: Thick rock and concrete absorb the radiation and stop material escaping, so people are neither irradiated nor contaminated.

core.p: Ionising radiation is useful (medicine, sterilising, smoke alarms, power) but always carries a risk. Decisions are made by comparing the **benefit** with the **risk**, and by keeping doses as low as possible.
bullets: A CT scan gives a larger dose than a chest X-ray, so it is only used when the extra information is needed.
The risk of cancer from a medical dose is small compared with the risk of not diagnosing or treating a serious illness.
Scientists' understanding of the dangers has grown over time: early workers such as Marie Curie handled sources without protection, and many suffered radiation-related illness.
Workers and the public have legal **dose limits**.

core.h: Key vocabulary to use in answers
core.p: Mark schemes reward specific words. Use them precisely and you will pick up easy marks.
bullets: Say radiation **ionises** atoms, not 'kills' atoms.
Say **DNA is damaged** or a **mutation** occurs, leading to **cancer**.
Use **irradiation** for exposure from outside and **contamination** for radioactive material on or in the body.
Say **absorbed**, not 'blocked', when explaining shielding.
Say the source is **in contact with** or **close to** cells when explaining why alpha is dangerous inside.

analogy.p: Irradiation is like standing in front of a fire: you get heated while you are near it, and you can step back, put up a screen or leave, and the heating stops. Contamination is like a hot coal falling into your pocket: it keeps burning you wherever you go until you get it out. An alpha source is like a coal that cannot burn through your coat, harmless outside but very damaging if it gets inside. Where it breaks down: heat warms everything evenly, whereas radiation causes random, invisible ionisation events, and damage such as cancer may appear years later rather than straight away.

terms.d: Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, forming ions.
The process of an atom gaining or losing electrons to become a charged ion.
A change in the DNA (genetic code) of a cell.
Uncontrolled division of cells, which can be caused by mutations in DNA.
Harm to a group of cells, for example burns or organ damage, when many cells are killed.
A measure of how much ionising radiation the body has absorbed; the greater the dose the greater the risk of harm.
Exposure to ionising radiation from a source outside the object or person; the object does not become radioactive.
The unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or inside an object or person.
Material such as lead or concrete placed between a source and people to absorb radiation.
A device worn by workers to measure the dose of radiation they have received.
Long-handled tools used to handle sources so the source is kept at a distance from the body.
Unwanted radioactive material, for example from nuclear power stations or hospitals.
The time taken for half the undecayed nuclei in a sample to decay, or for the activity to halve.
How far a radiation can travel through a material before being absorbed.
How strongly a radiation ionises the atoms it passes; alpha is the most ionising, gamma the least.

mistakes.w: Irradiated food becomes radioactive.
mistakes.r: Irradiation does not make an object radioactive; only contamination leaves radioactive material behind.

mistakes.w: Alpha is the least dangerous radiation.
mistakes.r: Alpha is least dangerous outside the body but most dangerous inside, because it is strongly ionising and all its energy is absorbed by nearby cells.

mistakes.w: Radiation kills atoms.
mistakes.r: Radiation ionises atoms and molecules, which can damage DNA or kill cells.

mistakes.w: Gamma is most dangerous inside the body because it is the most penetrating.
mistakes.r: Inside, gamma is less hazardous than alpha: it is weakly ionising and much of it passes out of the body.

mistakes.w: Wear a lead apron to stop contamination.
mistakes.r: Shielding reduces irradiation; contamination is prevented by gloves, protective clothing, masks and not touching the source.

mistakes.w: Use tongs so you do not get radiation on you.
mistakes.r: Tongs increase the distance between the source and the hand, so less radiation is absorbed; they also prevent contamination of the skin.

mistakes.w: Radiation causes cancer straight away.
mistakes.r: Radiation can damage DNA causing a mutation; the mutated cell may later divide uncontrollably, causing cancer.

mistakes.w: Radioactive waste is dangerous because it might explode.
mistakes.r: It is dangerous because it emits ionising radiation for a long time (long half-life) and could leak and contaminate water or food.

mistakes.w: Contamination and irradiation are the same thing.
mistakes.r: Irradiation is exposure from an outside source; contamination is radioactive material on or in the body that keeps irradiating you.

exam.q: State one way in which ionising radiation can harm the human body.
model: Any one: damages/kills cells or tissue; causes mutations in DNA; causes cancer.
exam.tip: One clear effect is enough; 'it is bad for you' scores zero.

exam.q: Explain how ionising radiation can cause cancer.
model: Radiation ionises atoms/molecules in cells
This damages DNA causing a mutation
Mutated cell divides uncontrollably (forming a tumour)
exam.tip: Use the chain: ionise, DNA, mutation, uncontrolled division.

exam.q: Describe the difference between irradiation and contamination.
model: Irradiation: exposure to radiation from a source outside the body/object
Contamination: radioactive material/atoms get on or into the body/object
exam.tip: Mention where the radioactive material is in each case.

exam.q: Food can be irradiated with gamma rays to kill bacteria. Explain why the food is safe to eat afterwards.
model: The food is irradiated, not contaminated / no radioactive material is left in it
So the food does not become radioactive / does not emit radiation
exam.tip: The key word is that irradiation does not make things radioactive.

exam.q: Explain why an alpha source is more dangerous inside the body than outside the body.
model: Outside: alpha is absorbed by the outer layer of skin/air
So it cannot reach living cells
Inside: the source is next to living cells
Alpha is strongly ionising so causes a lot of damage to those cells
exam.tip: Two marks for each situation; always link penetration for outside and ionising power for inside.

exam.q: A teacher uses a radioactive source in a lesson. Give two precautions the teacher should take and explain how each reduces the risk.
model: Handle the source with long tongs
Increases distance so less radiation absorbed by the hand
Store in a lead-lined box when not in use / minimise time out of box
Lead absorbs radiation / less time means fewer decays reach people
exam.tip: Precaution then reason, twice. Other valid pairs: never point it at anyone; wear gloves to prevent contamination.

exam.q: Hospital workers who use radiation wear a dosimeter badge. State why.
model: To measure/monitor the dose of radiation they receive (so it can be kept below a safe limit).
exam.tip: 'To protect them' is wrong: the badge measures, it does not shield.

exam.q: Radon is a radioactive gas that emits alpha particles. Explain why breathing in radon is a health risk.
model: The radon is inside the lungs / this is contamination
Alpha particles are strongly ionising
So they damage cells in the lungs, possibly causing cancer
exam.tip: Spot that gas being breathed in means contamination.

exam.q: Describe the problems of disposing of radioactive waste and how the risks can be reduced.
model: Some waste has a long half-life so stays radioactive for thousands of years
It could leak into groundwater/soil and contaminate food or water
Containers must last a very long time without corroding
High-level waste gets hot so needs cooling
Reduce risk by sealing in glass/concrete and steel containers
Store deep underground in geologically stable rock, away from people and water, and monitor the site
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need both halves: problems AND solutions, linked with 'so' and 'because'.

exam.q: A worker accidentally gets radioactive dust on their skin. Explain why this is more hazardous than standing near a sealed source for the same length of time.
model: This is contamination
The radioactive atoms are in contact with the skin/may be breathed in or swallowed
So exposure continues after leaving the area until removed or decayed (and alpha could reach cells)
exam.tip: The key idea is that contamination continues; irradiation stops when you move away.

worked.q: Three sources emit alpha, beta and gamma respectively. Which is most dangerous (a) held near the body, (b) swallowed? Explain.
steps: Outside the body, radiation must penetrate skin to reach living cells.
Alpha is stopped by skin; beta and gamma penetrate, and gamma penetrates furthest to internal organs.
(a) So gamma (or beta) is most dangerous outside.
Inside the body, all radiation starts next to living cells, so ionising power matters most.
Alpha is the most strongly ionising and all of its energy is absorbed by a small volume of nearby tissue.
(b) So alpha is most dangerous inside.
worked.ans: (a) Gamma (penetrates to organs); (b) alpha (most ionising and absorbed by nearby cells).

worked.q: Model answer: A student says 'a patient who has had a gamma ray treatment should stay away from other people because they are now radioactive.' Evaluate this statement.
steps: Identify the type of exposure: an external gamma beam is irradiation.
Irradiation does not leave radioactive material in the patient.
So the patient does not emit radiation after the beam is switched off.
Contrast: if the patient had swallowed or been injected with a radioactive substance, they would be contaminated and would emit radiation for a while.
Conclusion: the statement is wrong for external treatment.
worked.ans: The student is wrong: external treatment irradiates the patient but does not make them radioactive; only an internal (contaminating) source would.

worked.q: Applied example: list four precautions for a hospital technician preparing a radioactive injection, with a reason for each.
steps: Work behind a lead or lead-glass screen: lead absorbs radiation, reducing irradiation.
Use tongs or a syringe shield: keeps distance and absorbs radiation from the syringe.
Wear gloves and a lab coat: prevents radioactive liquid contaminating skin.
Wear a dosimeter badge: monitors dose so it stays below the legal limit.
Also: work quickly to minimise time.
worked.ans: Shielding, distance, protective clothing against contamination, and dose monitoring (plus minimum time).
